speechtext:
This bill proposes a certain number of amendments to the criminal code. I will merely indicate a few of them. First there are amendments suggested by the interprovincial conference that took place two or three months ago between the attorneys general of the various provinces in connection with stock market operations.
There is an amendment repealing certain sections of the criminal code concerning sedition. This is the same as that which has passed the [Mr. Hanson.)

now?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has heretofore afforded to our opponents the opportunity of making unwarranted criticisms which really have no weight whatsoever. In 1921, the people of Canada worried in many ways by the government of that day, desired ardently an era of peace. It was then that the present Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) put in his program as an outstanding feature, a promise of an era of peace, should the citizens of Canada entrust him with their confidence. No one, to-day, can state that the Prime

Minister failed to carry out his promise and that his efforts did not tend to ensure peace to this country. Because our neighbours, through their legislation, seem to express a desire of ceasing all trade with us, the Prime Minister, without any fuss directed the efforts of his government in negotiating with better disposed countries. On the other hand our opponents, if we are to believe them, would have preferred to see the government take part in a series of provocative tariff wrang-lings, forgetting that imported page of history, when England in 1775, on a simple tariff question, lost her wealthiest colony, the United States, and might also have lost Canada, had it not .been for the bullet of a valiant French-Canadian which laid low the brave General Montgomery, saved the situation and preserved the colony to the British Empire. These tariff changes may perhaps afford the opportunity to a few trade profiteers to squeeze for a time the people of this country, but their little sport will be of short duration since our relations with the West Indies and Bermuda, helped by our merchant marine equipped for the transport of fruits and vegetables will enable the government to improve conditions without much delay. The people must continue to trust the present government, if it wishes to enjoy peace in this country, and they can rest assured that if, one day, Canada is annexed to the United States the Liberal party's policy will not be to blame but the fault will be with the provoking methods of the Tory policy.
One question of which the present budget makes no mention, but which is very much alive, is that of the canalization of the St. Lawrence river. For some years it has been before the universities, the newspapers, the parliaments-as much American as Canadian -and in commercial circles under the title of "The Great Lakes Waterway," contemplating the canalization of the St. Lawrence to the head of the Great Lakes. In certain quarters this scheme is considered possible and practical. The Federation of Shippers, an association regarded as an authority in navigation, declares that the project is a serious error from the standpoint of navigation; the Chamber of Commerce of Montreal, a body composed of business men, opposes it from the economic viewpoint. But Ontario sees Toronto becoming an ocean port and Montreal a secondary harbour; the farmers of the west allow themselves to believe that the cost of shipping their grain will be made practically negligible; while others still more enthusiastic go to the length of hailing lake Superior as "the Mediterranean of the North!"

The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers
Numerous engineers come forward to present claims and opinions which are contradictory, and depend upon the party to which they belong.
However, from what we can deduce from official reports at our disposal, it seems to be agreed that the enterprise is practicable. I consider the question in the light of two factors, the time and the money. These reports and the supporters of the scheme tell us that navigation would be the principal objective and that the development of hydroelectric power would be secondary. However, setting to one side all these diverse opinions, interested or not, carefully studied, or not, I will consider this from the point of view of business and logic.
Starting from this point of view, I contend that the enterprise is not inspired by the actual needs of navigation, that the future holds out no promise of a time in which the project could be called necessary, and, moreover, that it cannot have navigation as its principal objective. Finally I say that the question of electrical power cannot be held a factor at present, since we have to deal with American financiers interested in the eastern part of the United States and who are at present engaged in figuring how they can lay a heavy hand upon our water-power resources for the benefit of their country.
Moreover, the completion of the project would not deal a death blow to the port of Montreal, nor abet the ambitions of Toronto, nor would it reduce in any degree the transportation costs of the western farmer. Thus, as it is a question involving an expenditure of probably a billion dollars, the greatest caution should be adopted before taking any decision, whether upon a joint enterprise or otherwise. It is the duty of the taxpayer, responsible already for two and one-half billion dollars of national debt, to study seriously what is proposed before committing himself.
Any person who knows anything, however little, of the history of his own country will admit that in the early days of colonization the St. Lawrence river was the only commercial artery, and that it rendered substantial service to the district through which it flowed. In later times it has continued to serve, but not alone, since it has shared the commerce with the railways. The progress, not alone of Canada, but of every country in the world, has imposed upon trade generally the necessity of rapid transportation, which has resulted in the development of the railways as carriers, a system of transportation more rapid, less
dear to insure, less exposed to weather hazards, going everywhere and at all times, so that transportation by water, especially in the canals, is very slow and does not possess any of the advantages of which the railways boast.
From these considerations we see, not only in Canada, but also in all other countries, a shrinkage in the volume of goods shipped by canal, while we see, on the other hand, the shipments by rail increase substantially, except in a few exceptional cases.
To emphasize this point-knowing that our canal systems are actually utilized only to 66 per cent of their capacity, considering that Fort Churchill in the future will divert a considerable volume of the grain of the West from the St. .Lawrence, that the development and steadily increasing accommodation of the harbours of Vancouver and Victoria will absorb more and more, notwithstanding the methodical reorganization of agriculture in Russia, the serious competition of Tcheco-slovakia, the southern republics and the Scandinavian countries-all these things are surely sufficient to Show that the existing canals are more than adequate. They force us to admit that we may look for a gradual diminution in the annual tonnage passing through our canals, since we know that half of cur western grain production goes through the United States by rail via Buffalo, even New York, at a greater cost of transportation, and that this condition will continue into the future. It surely is not possible for us, therefore, to give the need for wider transportation facilities on the St. Lawrence as the premier object of this enterpise, neither for the present nor for the future.
The need for water power cannot be urged on behalf of the project since Quebec and Ontario are exporting electrical energy by the hundreds of thousands of horse power to the United States, under yearly contracts which are susceptible of 'being cancelled from year to year if the provinces so desire.
Such is not the case with the Eastern states, the real ones behind the scheme and the only ones to derive any benefit from it, more particularly if they could get this power at half price after having inveigled us into paying half the cost of the undertaking.
The taxpayers always foot the bill and they should, in their own interests, learn and retain just what it costs to build these so-called seaway shipping canals; the methods and the results of these undertakings are, to my mind, always the same in all countries.
When the Panama Canal was first broached it was understood that the cost would be in

The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers
the neighbourhood of $100,000,000; but when the work was done people realized that it had cost $430,000,000. The Chicago canal, which according to the first estimates, could be completed for $16,000,000, cost all told $92,000,000. The Manchester canal cost 110 per cent more than the estimate, as did the Suez canal; the Welland canal, supposed to cost only $55,000,000, will have cost $115,000,000 or $120,000,000 before its completion.
This scheme, according to the engineers' first estimates, was to cost $252,000,000 (report of June 21, 1925). Later on this was revised to $6.50,000.000. Other engineers that I have consulted have told me that this undertaking might well cost one billion dollars or more. So we are perfectly justified in leaving a considerable margin in all these calculations, since these engineers' estimates have always been wide of the mark and the final cost has been two, three, even four times the original figure, despite the fact that the engineers responsible have been men with a well deserved reputation for science and workmanship.
Therefore the people of the country have fair warning that they are confronted with an undertaking of a kind that is always deceptive and decidedly expensive; that they should think well before going into an enterprise of that nature.
Let us say that our part of the cost will be $325,000,000 or one-half of $650,000,000; the yearly fixed charges will be a heavy burden for the public to bear. The annual interest at 4J per cent will be $14,625,000; maintenance and operation of a 25-foot canal will cost about $2,000,000 more; roughly a yearly total of $17,000,000 which in all likelihood will be near $20,000,000. While two economic factors which remain unchanged, time and transportation insurance, cause half of our Canadian wheat to be sent by rail through Buffalo via New York, it is nevertheless a fact that the quantity of wheat shipped to Montreal through our canals averages less than 100,000,000 bushels a year. But, speaking in a broad way, let us suppose that in 1935 we carry 400,000,000 bushels; it will require 4^ cents per bushel to meet the annual fixed charges of $17,000,000.
If, instead of building this canal for $650,000,000, with a yearly fixed charge of $17,000,000 for the transportation of 400,000,000 bushels of wheat, the government helped the farmers of the west with a bonus of two cents a bushel, at a total cost of S8,000,000, which implies that our present canal system would be utilized to only 50 per cent of its capacity, the one and only object of those who are behind this scheme, namely a reduction of two cents a bushel in the cost of our western wheat to

the seaboard would be attained and the government would save the balance of the $17,000,000 or $9,000,000. It' is quite evident that the government cannot accept this policy of a bonus which, would be class legislation of the worst kind; but the promoters have not yet succeeded in showing us that their scheme would bring about a reduction of two cents a bushel in the freight rates. On the contrary, it is more than likely that there will be no reduction whatever. That is what a business man, looking after his own interests, would do in like circumstances. Why should the public authorities not have recourse to the same solution, or else why should they have anything to do with such a scheme? We may readily conclude that the prime object of the enterprise is not navigation, which is more than amply provided for; we know that the proposed innovation would not result in lowering the freight rates; for corroboration we have only to look to the engineers' schedule of expenses where they allow 5-6 of the $650,000,000 for water-power development, which means 5-6 for the main object of the scheme power.
Of the total cost of $650,000,000 there is set aside the sum of $120,155,000 for digging a 25-foot canal. The Thousand Islands section is to cost $1,100,000; the international waterfalls $33,481,000; lake St. Francis, $980,000; Sou-langes $31,594,000, which represents the first group, Soulanges and Lachine forming the second.
Lachine would cost $53,000,000. According to the estimates the first group would yield 2,700,000 h.p., the second group 5 million h.p.
One could not choose a more inopportune time for such an undertaking; we have a population of barely nine millions, we are saddled with 22,000 miles of railway and our national debt is over two billions of dollars. At a time when our war taxes are still a heavy burden foreign speculators come here and try to talk us into accepting this w'hite elephant which will cost at the very least $500,000,000, while it is evident that our navigation system can well get along without it and that we have no need of additional water-powers. We are justified in making an appeal to common sense; for if we go into this thing without due reflection we are bound to pay the consequences.
We must necessarily take into account the opening a new seaport at Churchill with an objective exactly similar to that of the St. Lawrence which, at the start will be another burden on the Canadian taxpayer anl later will attract a considerable share of the St. Lawrence canal's business; also the C.N.R. and C.P.R. will lose a goodly part of their

The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers
profitable traffic between Georgian bay and Montreal; after all, our western grain can be shipped only once. The first part of the haul is by rail; and since the railroads will have had their receipts lessened for the benefit of the canal system they will eventually have to increase their freight rates on grain; so what the farmer gains on the one hand he sacrifices on the other, and in the end he'll be no better off.
Our canal system as it stands to-day, and it is used to only 50 per cent of its capacity, cost this country $250,000,000. When it was decided to build a canal 14 feet deep from Montreal to lake Superior those responsible foresaw a tremendous increase in traffic. Were their hopes justified? The reports of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics inform us that for a period of 19 years, from 1908-when we began to keep separate statistics for the traffic in American and in Canadian grain-up to 1926 inclusive, there has been a decrease in traffic. The reasons are not far to seek: they always are and always will 'be the same: quicker delivery and lower insurance rates. In other words the necessity of shipping the goods the quickest possible way and avoid high rates of insurance. Such is the business policy adopted throughout the entire world; and all the engineers' estimates will not change it one iota.
The federal statistics report shows clearly that during this period while water borne traffic decreased there was an increase in railway transport.
In 1913, 11,130,865 tons passed through our canals; in 1925, 9,750,311 tons; and in 1918, 3,369,474.
The difference in the volume of traffic is quite apparent. If we take an average for the five-year period from 1916 to 1921 it gives us 4,559,149 tons.
Let us divide that 19-year period into two parts, the first from 1908 to 1917 inclusively; the second from 1918 to 1926. We find that for the first part 78,197,080 tons passed through our canal, or an average of 7,819,708 tons per year.
During the second part, our canal traffic was 59,065,570 tons, an average of 6,451,752 tons, or a decrease of 4.7 per cent, as contrasted with the first part of the given period.
It cannot be claimed this was due to a general decrease in traffic because during the same period railway traffic increased tremendously. For the first 10 years from 1908 to 1917, our railroads carried 900,691,796 tons or an average per year of 90,069,179 tons for the latter part of this period that is, the nine years from 1917 to 1926, the total traffic
reached 1,037,903,947 tons, a yearly average of 114,211,550 tons. So while our canal system suffered a decrease in traffic of 4.7 per cent, our railroads were carrying 25 per cent more freight. This state of affairs was not characteristic of Canada but prevailed throughout the entire world with the one exception of the Panama Canal, which unites two oceans; this justified Prof. Milverton of Chicago in claiming that canals were a commercial error.
At any rate, this furnishes a powerful argument against those who would have us believe that the deepening of the St Lawrence to 25 feet is an urgent necessity. Following along the same line of reasoning we have the case of the Erie canal which serves quite aptly for purposes of comparison to the St. Lawrence project, as it runs through a highly industrialized region, and within the reach of the west, having a certain depth and capable of being further deepened. It would serve the same purpose that the promoters of the St. Lawrence canal have in mind, and perhaps with better chances of success. The aim which the New York state had in view was a canal of 25 feet in depth with prospects of controlling the output of the same territories included in the St. Lawrence scheme. The Senate and Congress unanimously voted $112,000,000 to put into execution this scheme; however, Symmons, an engineer of high repute, having the confidence of the authorities of his country refused to carry it out, qualifying it as a dream, he however deepened it by 5 to 12 feet and this cost double the amount voted. Events proved that he was right, be saved his country a considerable amount of money. Indeed, in the five or six years which followed the deepening of the canal to 12 feet, they did not transport one-fifth of the freight they carried when the canal was but 5 feet deep, and, in 1926, they were losing 80 per cent of the volume of freight, notwithstanding the improvement to the canal; this so astonished the Governor of New York, that he advised the closing of the canal or renting to private companies. This is an example to us showing that we should be careful, if the U.S. did not succeed, how can Canada do better.
The public must give their serious attention to our canal traffic. In 1926, 9,656,190 tons passed through our canal, of this total 3,340,000 tons were grain, 663,000 tons pulp, 351,000 tons sand, manufactured products 723,917 tons, and merchandise 251,066 tons. Machinery being considered as a negligible amount. It ia easily seen that the traffic was not very diversified and that the main portion waa grain.
The Budget-Mr. Deslauriers

be given our Canadian workmen since they know full well that a great part of this work
vill be done by machinery, that it will only last a limited time, and that once the thing is completed, since Canada has no need of it, and its advantages will accrue more to the U.S. than to Canada, that new industries will spring up on the other side of the border, and our working population will have less and less employment in Canada.
There is no need of counting on the increase in our population. The project is fallacious, on the face of it.
Competition on the grain markets cannot be adduced as an incentive to the realization of this canal project which will only increase our already-heavy annual burden of fixed charges as I have shown in the course of my remarks; it is an error to believe that an increase in the number of seaports necessarily indicates an increase in the volume of trade.
According to Mr. Thomas Robb, the deepening of the St. Lawrence would lower its level, consequently vessels would have to carry less grain; this is one side of the problem that the promoters have not touched.
At all events, if Canada had any capital to risk for the development of navigation, and of waterpowers, the opinion of Mr. Arthur Sur-veyer, hydrographic engineer, and the opinion of the Montreal Chamber of Commerce should prevail. Why should not this capital be applied to the development of the Georgian Bay scheme? I fail to see any reason.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman has exhausted the time at his disposal.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was my unhappy lot to be unable to follow the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Deslauriers) who has just taken his seat. No doubt there was much in his speech to merit attention and I would have been glad to follow and to attempt to answer his arguments.
May I refer to some words of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) which he used during his presentation of the budget:
All governments make expenditures on capital account and frequently such undertakings are carried out by the use of borrowed capital. With that practice I find no fault, but may I emphasize the fact that in the past seven fiscal years it has been possible to carry out all capital expenditures of the Dominion without borrowing.
The statement of the minister is quite true, but it would have been fairer for the minister to have added that in the first year of this government's operations, eight years ago, it was obliged to borrow a very considerable

sum of money, and in so doing added to the funded debt of the country. I do not for one moment criticize the action of the government in that regard, since it was necessary to do so just as it was necessary for the preceding government to take a similar course on account of large expenditures caused by war and demobilization, and reorganization and consolidation of the Canadian National Railways. It is equally true that during the term of the preceding government, with the exception of the fiscal year 1920, in which ordinary capital expenditures were abnormal to the extent of $55,000,000 on account of extraordinary conditions caused through an unusual amount of money being required for the government railways and for government shipbuilding program, the same state of affairs obtained as that about which the finance minister now boasts. In those years the surpluses in consolidated fund compared more than favourably with those acquired by the government now in power. In each of the six years of the Union government the average surplus was $67,000,000 as compared with an average of $65,000,000 during the first six years in which this government has held office. It is true that surpluses of the last two years have changed the average somewhat in favour of the present government. An analysis however of surpluses during the whole eight years of their term will show that they averaged the amount of $67,000,000 annually, which is similar to the figure shown for the Union government. In addition we must remember that the present government has had a very substantial advantage because of the fact that special receipts to the amount of $45,436,000 have been placed in the treasury as compared with $2,224,800 during the term of the preceding government. The figure which obtained during the regime of the Union government was $2,224,800, while during the regime of the present government the special receipts have totalled $45,436,000.
Some credit has been taken by the government for the fact that $80,000,000 was retired last year; it was inferred by members opposite that that amount of money had been retired from the current surplus of the government. Of course that statement is not true. Part of it was retired from that source but the great bulk of it was retired from the money in the hands of the government at the commencement of this year. Members of the government, and particularly the Prime Minister, are fond of commenting on the great additions to the net debt incurred by the government which preceded the present one claiming that this

The Budget-Mr. Geary
was caused by the method of financing of that government. They make this claim in order to show that when they assumed office they were faced with financial difficulties. Such a statement has always appeared to me to be grossly unfair. Additions to the net debt during the six years of the preceding government were caused purely and simply by the necessity of providing money for purposes of war and demobilization and for the development of the national railways throughout the period of acquisition and consolidation. Under these headings the expenditures were:
Union	Present
government government War demobilization. $1,461,999,000 $ 7,711,000 Advances to railways	 209,672,000	131,509,000
In addition to that, in 1920 the preceding government took the bold step of including in the net debt of this country some $284,000,000 which was transferred to non-active assets and thereby increased the national debt. These non-active assets, previously being active assets, had formerly operated in the reduction of the net debt. Advances to government railways, of course, always had been earned as non-active assets. It will be seen, therefore, that the preceding government incurred capital expenditures which ordinarily might have been added to the debt of this country, to the following extent:
War demobilization	$1,461,999,804
Railways	 209,671,940
Advances to railways transferred to non-active assets.. 284,015,005

As against that vast amount of money, the net debt of the country increased by only $1,806,979,630. Thus there was a difference of $148,707,119 by which in effect the preceding government reduced out of current revenue the debt, which otherwise might have been added to the debt of the country.
In the present budget the Minister of Finance takes credit for the fact that this government has carried* through all capital expenditures and railway advances out of the ordinary revenue of the government. The fact upon which I want to lay emphasis-and it is a fact-is that this government in that regard has not done so well as the preceding Union government, despite all the disadvantages under which that government laboured. When we consider that in addition to ordinary revenue the present government has had the advantage of some $43,000,000 in special receipts more than the preceding government
had, it will be readily seen that the Union government was able to achieve more towards the reduction of the net debt of the country during its six years of office than the present government has been able to do in the eight years it has been in power.
The only refuge left to the Prime Minister in this matter is the statement that the railway expenditures of the preceding government should not be credited, and his reason for making this statement is that these were advances to a railway which was not a going concern and was not paying its way. His statement is that advances which have been made by this government have been advances to a going concern which is paying its way. This is not a fair answer, because it is well known that advances such as those made during the process of reorganization are strictly capital account. The position is somewhat analogous to that occupied by a firm constructing a building; interest on the moneys expended on construction properly take their place in capital account. Moreover, in spite of what the Prime Minister has said, the present government has followed exactly the same course, for in 1923 it charged $77,863,938.23 and in 1924 $23,710,616.70 as advances to the Canadian National Railways, which advances were not made to a railway which was a going concern and paying its way, because in those two years the Canadian National Railways were not doing anything of the kind. In addition, whatever may be the merits or demerits of the system of accounting in force in this country, this government has guaranteed the payment of vast sums which have been borrowed by the Canadian National Railways. These may not be a direct liability, but certainly they are a secondary liability, and these latter amounts must be considered as something of an addition to the debt of the country.
My object in putting these figures on Hansard, Mr. Speaker, is to show that the claims of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are absolutely unfounded in this regard and that the financial record of this government not only is not better than the financial record of the government which preceded it, but is worse by many millions of dollars in the net result.
A surplus always has been a matter of importance to the present government; it has loomed large in its calculations and has been used invariably as an asset in its appeal to the country. For many years there has been a surplus, that is, an amount of money which is available for the reduction of the debt of the country. In connection with one article
The Budget-Mr. Geary

alone, tea, this government in the last five or six years has taken probably $15,000,000 in taxes directly from the pockets of people of all classes in this country.
That amount of money never has been required to form a surplus or to make ends meet. The tax was put on first as a war measure, not as a protective measure in any sense of the word, and it was only because of the desire of the government to show a handsome surplus at the end of its fiscal year that it did not long ago remove that tax. I say that during the past five years at least the government, with no justification whatever, has taken from the pockets of the people, through a tax perhaps more evenly distributed than any other, this large amount of money which it might very well have foresworn years ago. If anything were required to indicate that this budget is purely for election purposes it is the fact that on the eve of an election the government has seen fit at last to remedy that injustice and to remit to the people that tax which long ago they should have been forgiven.
Speaking generally of the budget, it is quite plain that it is not founded on conviction or principle, but that the basis of the whole concoction is simply this: "How can we so build up this budget as to attract votes in the impending election?" The presentation of the budget was deferred until much later in the session than usually is the case, and it did not take final form until an election had been decided upon. It is quite obvious, of course, that the government must have known that it is in growing disfavour with the people of this country, because of its futility and its indecision in tariff matters, and also because there has been spreading a very well defined feeling and conviction on the part of the people that the government has been far too sensitive to the moods and views of the people of the United States. On the whole, things were going very badly for the government, and it was decided to make of the budget if possible such a gesture as would disarm the criticism which had arisen in many quarters. Further delay undoubtedly was caused by the efforts which were necessary to overcome the reluctance of certain members of the government to stultify themselves and their followers as needs they must in supporting such a budget. However, he that will use all winds must shift his sail, and in the end the thing was accomplished.
Now I fear that , the government finds that it has been just a little too clever and has overreached itself, and that the people of this country, whom it hoped to hoodwink, continue to see. They have examined the 
budget; they have examined the proposals and the claims made in regard to them and they have become fully aware of the weaknesses of the structure. They recognize the inconsistency of those who propose these measures and, in the words of the amendment, have lost confidence in the government and recognize from its past course and its present action that it is not to be entrusted with the direction of the fiscal policy of this country. The people of Canada want straight dealings and definite policies; they do not approve of mere smartness and supposedly clever political manoeuvres in the conduct of their business. The very best day the government had in regard to this budget was the day it was printed in the newspapers. Since then, every day and in every way the budget has continued to lose favour with the people. For instance, it was thought by the framers of the budget that the headlines which would naturally follow the declaration that 270 items had been added to the free list under the British preference would be of some advantage in a campaign. On the day of publication it may have had some effect, but from day to day it lost its appeal. It could not stand the test of examination; for instance it was found that of those 270 items the majority affect commodities in which there either never has been any trade with England, and is not at present any trade, or in which no one expects that there will be any trade. The prospects of increased trade are so vague and flimsy that no one in his senses will expect any benefits to be derived therefrom. It may be considered quite proper to put in the British preference such articles as hay and natural gas, but it is idiotic of the government to think that the people of this country are so unintelligent as to be deceived by claptrap of that kind.
As was stated by the Minister of Finance, protection is being given to the iron and steel industry because it is necessary to maintain an efficient and self-contained iron and steel industry in the Dominion of Canada; in the view of the government that could be done only by the imposition of a protective tariff. I would ask members of the government to consider what they have said in days gone by, to consider how they controverted this idea from beginning to end, to remember how they derided it; attempted to tear it to tatters, made fun of it and abused it in every possible way. It is not so long since we heard the boast made by a member of the government that the Liberal budget was ringing out the death knell of protection. If I read this budget rightly, it would seem to be ringing out a peal of welcome. The government conversion

The Budget-Mr. Geary
has been thorough and sudden and compared to it I should say that the incident of Saul of Tarsus was of the slow motion variety. If there is a national necessity to maintain a self-contained and efficient iron and steel industry in this country, is there not equally a national necessity to maintain a proper, efficient and self-contained textile industry?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And a furniture industry.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is there not a national necessity to maintain a self-contained copper industry, as well as to maintain many -other kinds of industry? . Does it not follow that in the view of the government the only way in which these industries can be maintained in an efficient and self-contained manner is by the application of the doctrine of protection? Why does not the government follow this new faith to the logical conclusion? We have heard the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Edwards), give us a very able exposition of the state of the textile industry in this country showing the need for protection. We have heard the excellent speech delivered by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fansher). With much of that speech I am unable to agree, but the hon. member gave many reasons for the support of the proposition that the government had in a backhanded way done that which it was afraid openly to do-increased the protection to the cotton industry. All this shows the inconsistency of the course of the government in dealing with matters of tariff.
When the question is asked: Why does not the government follow its new faith to the logical conclusion, there is only one answer, an obvious one: the government has no principle or conviction in the matter; its whole course is decided by the desire to obtain votes. The government asked itself the question: How can we frame a budget which will bring us votes?
It has been said both by one of the hon. members for Winnipeg and by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), that this is a budget which will appeal to different sections of the country. I always understood that this administration was following the plan of saying something special and different in each part of the country, and an hon. member opposite is reported in Hansard' as saying that it has sought to inquire into the needs of the various sections of Canada and to meet those needs by the proper remedies. How on earth are we going to meet the needs of the western provinces by the application of duties which will affect an industry in Nova Scotia?	We are	all agreed that the
application of a tariff does not affect
only the industry which receives the benefit therefrom, but it affects everyone either directly or indirectly.
The government has heretofore fought the claims of the producers of fruit and vegetables. For some time it acceded to the demands made by my hon. friends opposite, who wanted every semblance of protection to be taken away from fruit and vegetables. At their behest the government abolished or cancelled the order in council which gave seasonal protection to the growers of fruits and vegetables. That was a glorious victory for my hon. friend whom I see smiling across the way. On that day the sun shone bright in Weyburn, soft, balmy airs caressed the fevered brow of the worthy representative of that district (Mr. Young). All was lovely. Then from the blue sky came the thunderbolt of duties, a tariff was iput on fruit and vegetables. Luck was not with my hon. friend that day.

They have four tariffs
now instead of three.

speechtext: He will swallow that.

speechtext: The hon. member found that not only had the government done a right about face on the proposition, but it had gone mad or crazy in its application. It had clamped on a duty which was unnecessary from the standpoint of the producer, and the prices of vegetables rose over night. The government did not restrict the entry of vegetables which might compete with the pro ducers of British Columbia or of other sections of the country, but it restricted the import of fresh fruits and vegetables during that portion of the year in which we do not produce.

Still the hon. member will
vote for the budget.

speechtext:
I am not so sure about that. Listen to what the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) said last year, as reported on page 943 of Hansard:
I submit it would be a crime to compel him -the farmer-to pay more than he now does for the fruit he wishes to purchase for the benefit of his family.
Hear the pearls of wisdom which fell from the lips of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young), as reported on page 1208 of Hansard of last year.
All this talk about the importation of fruit and vegetables breaking the home market and ruining our own producers is arrant nonsense.
He also declared in effect that it was infamous to put duties on these particular articles, and still he sits there smiling.
The Budget-Mr. Geary

speechtext: And he is satisfied with this budget.

speechtext: Perhaps he is not so comfortable, because I do not think he has finally dissuaded himself from the course he followed. He is undecided if he will pursue the course which his conscience tells him to.

speechtext: Let his conscience be his guide.	.

speechtext: I do not intend to take any guidance from the other side of the house.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear also what the hon.
member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) said of a kindred matter:
-but if we place a tariff on this butter, one of two things will happen: we shall have to divert milk from those high priced markets to other sources or the people of Canada will have to go back to conditions which prevailed when our Conservative friends were in power, when they had to eat oleomargarine, a mixture of intestinal fats and southern oils imported largely from the United States.
And now my hon. friend will be forced to say that the blow came from his own friends. A duty is placed on New Zealand butter and properly too.
Taking the two groups alone: iron and steel, fruit and vegetables, I would ask: Does the action of the government commend itself to my friends from the prairie provinces? What think ye of it, ye men of the golden west? Have you any longer confidence in the professions, declarations or promises of a government which has shown itself so susceptible to the exigencies of political profit? If the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) were in his seat, I would ask him: Has the great apostasy been accomplished and has he in turn become an apostle of the new faith? It will be interesting to watch these hon. gentlemen vote. I should like to know where are the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), the Minister of Railways (Mr. Crerar), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). These were the four horsemen of the free trade apocalypse. They were found in the van of the struggle and rallying to their flag were such men as the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Bock). Where are they to-day? They have relegated themselves to that inconspicuous and ignoble position in the rear which is generally occupied by those known as camp followers.
With Liberalism betrayed, are the Liberals now to accept as the price of their adherence to the present government the hopes and ex-
LMr. Geary.l
pectations to be gathered from a wholly illusory increase in the British preference? Those proposals have, I think, been sufficiently analyzed and I do not know that I can take them up any further with advantage to the house. I did go through at some pains to myself, for I am not good at that sort of thing, the first two pages of the new tariff and in practically every case I found Great Britain was unable to compete to any extent with importations from other countries. Great Britain had, for instance, a 7t per cent differential on ploughs or drills, I do not remember which it was, and they could ship to Canada only $267 worth as opposed to $1,000,000 worth shipped to us by the United States. In another case, pumps, with a differential of 10 per cent they could not make any headway at all, obtaining trade to the extent of $247 out of a total of $1,783,497. That differential has been increased in some cases, but does anyone suppose, when with a 7i per cent or 10 per cent differential they could do no business, they could do any large trade with increases in the differential which are here proposed?
Let me refer to an article of table use like crockery and china. The object of the budget, as I understood the claims made, is to divert trade from what my friends across the floor insist upon calling the natural course of north and south, although I entirely disagree with them in that contention, and to make it flow east and west. The government found that the former avenue of trade was blocked by the actions of the United States and it decided to take certain trade away from the United States and give it to Great Britain. The only article in the lot where there seems to me to be any definite preponderance of trade with the mother country is that, of crockery and chinaware. We have no industiy worth speaking of, so I am informed, manufacturing these articles, and we export nothing. We import something like $2,500,000 worth from Great Britain; we import $91,000 worth from the United States and still, apparently, by this budget we are trying to take trade away from the United States and give it to Great Britain. If any trade is diverted, it will be from countries like Czechoslovakia and France with which we have by treaty solemnly agreed to trade.
It would not, as I say, be of any advantage to go again into a discussion of these items, but may I say just one other word following my examination of the first two or three pages, that the only article in which British preference countries have any trade at all-

The Budget-Mr. Kennedy
and it was a very considerable trade-is butter. On the first three pages that is the only article on which they have not increased the British preference to give Great Britain more trade, but they have raised the duty and lessened the preference in order to shut off the trade in this article from the British dominions. The policy of the government was supposed to be to encourage trade with the British dominions, but they certainly did not believe in increasing this particular duty the night before they presented this budget. These illusory hopes and expectations of increased British import trade are what the western provinces have been given for the betrayal of their interests and as the price of their adherence to the government. These hopes and expectations are "such stuff as dreams are made on," and I have not the slightest doubt they will come to nothing. To adopt in part the same quotation, these hopes, expectations and promises of a future benefit, like the baseless fabric of this vision, shall dissolve and leave not a rack behind.
The Minister of Finance himself thinks very little of the British preference. By very plain inference and implication he says so when he warns the British people in his budget speech, lest he be trapped later by the discovery of how little it means; that they cannot do any trade with us even under these increased preferences unless they revise their methods of marketing and selling. For a small amount of trade that is potential or even for the larger amount that these visionaries think will eventuate, the British merchant has to remodel his whole selling system; he has to make a long study covering a period of years of the markets of this country, revise his whole packaging, shipping and selling system and all for what nobody by the closest and most optimistic scrutiny of the budget can declare in dollars to be of any substantial advantage.
It is not so long ago since we heard hon. members opposite talking of what a heinous offence it would be for this country to retaliate against the United States. I suppose a rose by any other name will smell as sweet, and perhaps retaliation will, when you call it countervailing, Countervailing is nothing but setting up against, and if setting up against is not retaliation, I do not know what retaliation is. Very properly, from their point of view, hon. members opposite inveighed against this principle during last session and this sesion. We have heard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) refer to it. As reported on page 1338 of Hansard, 1929, he said:
Talk of red blood! Is it a manifestation of red blood to shape our tariff policies on the policies of foreign countries by imitation or in any other manner?
Yet the Minister of Justice sat in conclave with the other members of the government when they foreswore their convictions and principles in this regard and made up a vote-catching budget that reflected nothing whatever of sincerity in its makeup. The question is: Have we or have we not confidence in the methods and practice of policy of the government? Unhesitatingly I say the answer of the country to that will be: No, we have not confidence. How can the house, how can the country, profess confidence in a government whose whole history has been a denial of consistency, whose course in fiscal policy has been one of devious ways, whose lack of conviction and of principle is painfully apparent, who stand ready at all times to sink their faith, if any they have, in the sea of expediency.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this occasion with some hesitation to speak on the budget and the two amendments that are before the house. It would be quite impossible for me, in view of what has happened during the past ten days, to say that I have any very definite opinion upon the details of the budget. I must confess some admiration for those people throughout the length and breadth of Canada and some in the old land who were able to tell us within twenty-four hours of the presentation of the budget just what it meant. However, I have come to some conclusions with regard to the budget, and these I shall present to the house in the time at my disposal.
Before proceeding to comment on the budget itself, I wish to make a few comments on another question which is really of greater importance than the budget itself, judging by the effect which it has had on the house, and that is as to the conditions under which the government asks us to pass judgment on the budget and the rest of the business that we have to do this session. I refer, of course, to the announcement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that there is to be an election, and his invitation to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) to meet him to ascertain if it would not be possible to speed up and hastily get rid of the rest of the business that is before the house. The date of the Imperial economic conference was set some time last autumn, according to the speech from the throne, from which I quote:
In the summer of last year, an invitation was extended by His Majesty's government in Canada to all His Majesty's other governments to participate in an imperial economic conference in Canada at the earliest possible date. It was found that the convenience of the
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy

majority of the governments could best be met by an arrangement to hold the Imperial economic conference along with the Imperial conference in London in the early autumn of the present year. This has accordingly been arranged.
I maintain that in view of the fact that it was known last autumn that the Imperial economic conference was to be held this autumn it was utterly ridiculous to delay calling this house to meet until the 20th of February, to sit until the 11th of April and then adjourn until the 28th of April, present the budget, a very contentious budget, of course, containing a number of changes, meaningful or meaningless, on the 1st of May, and then to say six days after:	It is time to
have an election, and we had better arrange to get through the business of the session in an orderly, but in any case a hasty, manner. I do not know what the other members of this house think, but I am just giving it as my opinion that no member has any right to accept his $4,000 indemnity if he agrees to the suggestion as it was made by the Prime Minister, as I understand it. It seems to me that ordinary commonsense would have dictated to the Prime Minister, if there was even a suspicion in his mind that it was necessary to go to the country this year, that the opening of the session should not have been delayed beyond the first or second week in January at the latest. If a farmer anywhere in Canada conducted his business with as Ittle regard for times, events and seasons he would be in the sheriff's hands inside of twelve months. The management or mismanagement of this matter must rest with the Prime Minister, and to me it looks at present like a very bad case of mismanagement. In Hansard of May 6, 1930, the Prime Minister is reported as follows at page. 1835:
Under the circumstances, I would suggest to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that he and I meet together as soon as may be convenient to him to see if we cannot come to some agreement whereby the business of this present session can be brought to an orderly and speedy conclusion. It would be my wish to meet as well with my friend the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) and discuss with him the matters which he -would wish to have considered for the group which he leads and for those who sit about him.
Then he goes on to tell of the business of parliament. What is the situation? I do not think that we have voted one-third or even one-quarter of the estimates. I think we have gone into only two departments, and I do not believe the estimates of one department have been entirely voted yet. Then we have the budget before us. According to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), it makes very extensive changes which surely merit [Mr. Kennedy.}
careful analysis. Here we have the statement of the finance minister regarding the iron and steel schedules:
The iron and steel schedule is now an entity, compact and orderly, consisting of a single group of three hundred and twenty-five items. I have not attempted to refer in detail to all individual commodities affected, but only those of greatest interest. Details of each item will, of course, be dealt with in committee of ways and means.
Summarizing numerically I may say that under the iron and steel schedule general tariff rates have been reduced on sixty-six items and increased on forty.
Under the intermediate tariff, the reductions number eighty-six, and the increases twenty-four.
Under the British preferential tariff, the rates have been increased in eight cases and reduced, or made free, in one hundred and fifty-two.
They number something like 350 changes. In the budget of 1928, about 124 tariff items were struck out and 170 inserted; 4 new drawback items were added. In the budget of 1929, 17 items were struck out, 33 new items inserted, 12 drawback items struck out and 2 new ones inserted, and the sessions of 1928 and 1929 ran from four to five months. Here is a contentious budget, much more contentious I think than the budgets of 1928 or 1929, and after sitting less than three months we are asked apparently to get through with the whole thing in a hurry in order that we may have an election. Whether or not there should be an election this year is a matter that the government has decided, but I submit that in view of the fact that the session of 1929 closed some time in June, and the government having a mandate until November, 1931, it was an absolutely ridiculous proposition for the Prime Minister, after letting six weeks of the new year go by without calling the house after agreeing to two weeks' adjournment at Easter, after we had been sitting for less than three months to come to the house and say:	Let us get
through with this budget and the rest of the legislation before parliament, including the large volume of estimates that have not yet been touched, in as short a time as possible so that we can go to the country and hold an election before the economic conference. That is, having regard to the time the last session ended, and having proper regard to the work of the Imperial economic conference, here is seven months' business that we have utterly failed properly to arrange time for. The Prime Minister calls for orderly consideration of the business before us after making an announcement that is just about as conducive to orderly conduct of the business of the house as a nest of hornets would be to a man driving a string of mules.

speechtext:
Then, of course, we have the question of the staff of the House of Com-irions. A large number of the staff engaged around the House of Commons are paid by the day, and it is utterly unfair to them to close the session so abruptly. IVe have heard a *great deal about the government being a fnodel employer of labour. I do not think there is anything to indicate that the salaries of the temporary staff around the House of Commons are at all out of line with what they might be earning if they were engaged the year round. Here is another case where the announcement of the Prime Minister apparently has overlooked their interests and considered the one thing only, political expediency. During the last two or three years we have heard a good deal about an increase in the sessional indemnity; it has been discussed quietly around the house and in the country. I believe if the farmer members of the house could get home every year for seeding-and it would not be an impossibility- they would be better off with a decreased indemnity than with the present indemnity and sessions ending in June. But this year, if we have an indecisive election on top of this Lurried session, it will be necessary to hold a session between the election and the Imperial conference, and so far as the western farmer members are concerned, regardless of what group they belong to, they will be subject to the very great inconvenience of coming to Ottawa during the harvest season; and certainly, if you take a farmer member away from his farm in seed time and harvest, his sessional indemnity is far from being adequate. But the whole trouble is due to the utter mismanagement by the Prime Minister and the government with regard to the date of calling parliament together and the introduction of the budget so late in the session. This system under which one man at the head of a party can spring an election on the country at any time it suits him is altogether wrong and out of date.
Another matter I wish to comment on, Mr. Speaker, is the practice of going to the country every four years. The statute provides that there must be an election every five years. But that statutory provision is of absolutely no value, either to parliament or to the government, so far as I can see; it only provides
14, 1930 2081
The Budget-Mr. Kennedy
opportunity for the sort of juggling that we have had during the past few months. If the practice of going to the country every four years is continued, why not so provide in the statute? If the present practice is not to be continued, why not observe the statutory provision and go to the country every five years? At least once we had the matter on a definite basis the government would not be able to excuse themselves for such a mess as we are in at the present time with regard to the business of the session. I was very glad to hear the leader of the opposition although he appealed on two occasions for an election, state on the floor of this house that so far as the budget was concerned he would not agree to passing it without making a careful scrutiny and without being supplied with full information in regard to all the items. As members of parliament I do not think we have any right to hurry through the business of the country on account of the pending Imperial conference or any other matter. In this regard I think we might say that things should be done decently and in order, especially when there was ample opportunity to make proper arrangements ahead of time. It seems to me that the Prime Minister with his various veiled announcements regarding the possibility of an election is mainly responsible for the feeling of uncertainty respecting an election which, last week, he said existed throughout the country. In the course of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne we had his announcement that there might be an election. Then of course everybody began to speculate. But even at that time if the government had had a definite policy regarding an appeal to the country, and had stated their intention, I think no one would have complained much against them in taking that position, and I think they would have been justified in doing so. But it seems to me that party exigency has been the ruling motive, and that the welfare of the country has been sacrificed for the sake of the Liberal party. I do not know whether this course of action is going to do the party any good; I think it will be the reverse.
Now, coming directly to the budget itself, I suppose it is correct to say that it is a protectionist budget. I think anyone who has followed the discussions before the tariff board must come to the conclusion that the steel interests appealed to the board for such a tariff as would effectively protect them from United States competition. In the course of his budget speech, at page 1625 of Hansard, the minister said:

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to devote my
attention more particularly to the subamendment now before the house. I agree with that part of the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Fan-sher) which states that it is to be regretted that more effective consideration has not been given to the position of agriculture and labour, but I cannot agree with the latter part of the subamendment which states that the best interests of Canada would be served by a substantial increase in the British preference, particularly with reference to textiles.
You may examine these tariff proposals with a microscope, but I suggest that it will be impossible to find therein any provision whatever which will give one day's additional employment to any workman in the province

The Budget-Mr. Cohan
of Quebec or which will promote the prosperity of that province to the extent of a single dollar, if you will except the provision with respect to the repeal in October next of the order in council giving free entry to New Zealand butter, which step has been so long demanded by the Conservative party.
I will show later, if I have time, that the proposed countervailing duties against vegetables and fruits from the United States should have been a seasonal tariff. Under this new tariff the difficulties which have been faced for years by the thousands of market gardeners on the island of Montreal through competition with the United States will be increased a hundredfold by the free admission of fruits and vegetables from the West Indies. There fruits and vegetables are produced by native labourers who live in houses which require no coal for their heating; whose clothing consists of leather or canvas sandals and cotton garments which cost no more than ordinary overalls, and who live largely on the native products of the country. These native labourers receive about one-fourth the wage of the ordinary agricultural labourer on the island of Montreal, and the products of that labour, which will be admitted free in quantities of hundreds of tons as soon as they discover that this market is free to them for the future, can be laid down in the city of Montreal at prices with which the Canadian producer cannot possibly compete. They have the cheapest freight rates on the Atlantic from those islands, and the ships which will carry their products will be subsidized to the extent of 81,750,000 from the treasury of Canada for the purpose of giving them access to an open market in this country in competition with our own growers of vegetables and fruits.
I should like to deal at greater length with this question if I had time, but I wish to discuss particularly the suggestion that the best interests of Canada would be served by a substantial increase in the British preference, particularly with regard to textiles. To-day the textile industry is a large factor in providing employment in the cities of Montreal, Verdun, Sherbrooke, Drummondville, Three Rivers and Shawinigan Falls, and is the chief source of employment in Valleyfield, Magog and Montmorency, all in the province of Quebec. The hon. member for York-Sun-bury (Mr. Hanson) last evening referred to similar factories in the province of New Brunswick at St. John, Marysville and Milltown. There are also similar factories at Cornwall, Ontario, and elsewhere, but I am now particularly concerned with the province of Quebec, one of whose constituencies I represent in this house.
The manufacture of cotton is essentially a Quebec industry. The latest report of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics shows that in the calendar year 1927, out of 39 establishments engaged in cotton cloth and yarn manufacturing in Canada, 17 were located in Quebec. Those factories employed 14,221 workers out of a total of 21,383 employed in the industry generally. They paid 811,197,832 in salaries and wages out of a total of 817,146,927 paid by the cotton cloth and yarn mills of Canada during that year.
In the revision of the Canadian cotton tariff schedule in 1928, the duty on imports of print cottons from the United States was reduced 5 per cent. The duty was left 2^ per cent lower than the duty on coloured cotton, although the manufacturing expense in printing cotton is considerably higher than in ordinary dyeing. This constitutes one of the most unreasonable tariff revisions ever attempted in the tariff history of this country. The tariff board took no evidence in support of this revision, and the reduction was not justified. It has reduced employment in the mills of the province of Quebec and has brought great loss and impending disaster to the cotton and woollen mills of Canada. Canadian cotton mills which are now operating at less than 60 per cent of their capacity, as well as on a non-profit basis, could easily and profitably maintain the present basis of prices for cotton goods to the Canadian consumer if the imports were restricted and their operations and employment were permitted to be carried on at or nearly at a capacity basis. Such a policy would immediately add several thousands to the list of those employed in Canada and would correspondingly increase the weekly payroll and thus materially assist in improving the current business situation throughout Canada.
Cotton mills in the province of Quebec are operating with reduced staffs for only three or four days a week, while some 1,500 or more cotton mill workers are at present unemployed. Sales volumes are down considerably and a great deal of the business at present taken by the mills to maintain even limited operations is being taken at a loss. The cotton industry is now operating at the lowest ebb of production and profits that has obtained for many years.
I wish the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) was in her seat, because I think the following facts should receive her consideration. The provincial laws r'f Quebec
20S6
The Budget-Mr. Cahan

very properly prescribe certain hours of labour; they preclude the employment of children and limit employment of women at night to two nights per week until nine o'clock, the aggregate not to exceed thirty nights in the whole year. Some of the Texas mills, whose products compete in the Canadian market with the Quebec mills, operate both night and day shifts of 55 hours each per week, as compared with a maximum of 50 hours per week in the Canadian mills. The night shift in a Texas mill generally consists of at least 75 per cent of female workers, and in many of the mills in the southern states children are employed for long hours. The minimum wage paid in the southern mills is about two-thirds of the minimum wage paid in Canada.
There is a still more striking contrast between the wages paid in Lancashire, England, and those paid in the cotton mills of the province of Quebec. This comparison shows the wages received for similar work performed on similar machinery in the same working hours:

those paid in the factories in the province of Quebec. It is in favour of such cheap labour that we give the Lancashire mills a preference in the Canadian market.
It is estimated by reliable authorities that importations account for over 40 per cent of the cotton manufactures and over 70 per cent of the woollen cloth manufactures consumed in Canada annually. During the past ten years, when these industries have been passing through a process of drastic competition and readjustment, not only have the Canadian mills been forced to meet the competition of excess stocks of British and foreign mills which were thrown on to the export markets at non-profit prices, but successive downward revisions of the British preferential, special treaty rates, the intermediate and general tariff rates in 1922, 1923 and 1928, have intensified, increased and widened this competition until the Canadian mills are now on the verge of disaster. The past year was one of the most competitive in the history of these industries, and the result has been that Canadian mills have operated at less than two-thirds of capacity, while the woollen cloth mills have fared even worse in the very limited market at their disposal, operating only three and four days a week and with reduced staffs. The worsted cloth weaving industry, which was presumed to have benefited by reason of the

duty-free yarns revision of the tariff in 1928, has reached the stage of over-productive capacity and non-profit margins. The cotton industry of the United Kingdom, which is developed to the basis of one spindle to each one of the population, and organized to export 85 per cent of its production, has lost 50 per cent of its export business due to the expansion and development of the cotton industry in India, China, Japan and other countries which were formerly large importers of cotton goods. The production of 20,000,000 spindles in the United Kingdom has thereby been thrown on the world markets. Reorganization is proceeding. The greatest combination of cotton mills in history, the Lancashire Cotton Corporation, is in process of formation. Bankrupt mills are being purchased at slaughter values. Hundreds of cotton mills in Lancashire have been closed. And now the Lancashire cotton industry, on the basis of reduced wages, reduced capital expends and non-profit margins, is striving to gain command of the Canadian market.
Here in Canada, the cotton industry is developed on the basis of one spindle to every eight of population. While in Canada, the British preferential rate on grey cottons is 12J per cent and on white cottons 15 per cent, in India, once Lancashire's greatest export market, the tariff on imports of cottons from the United Kingdom is 15 per cent and this in spite of the fact that wages in Canada are double those paid in Lancashire mills, whereas wages in the Indian mills are only about one-third those paid in Lancashire. Some 80 per cent of the Indian mills are said to be owned or controlled by English capital; yet there is no agitation throughout India in favour of creating a customs preference in favour of British cotton products.
In the United States the cotton manufacturing industry has an over-productive capacity and is seeking a slaughter market in Canada. There the industry is developed on the basis of one spindle to every two and a half of population, without facilities for increasing its export trade except on a slaughter basis.
The development of cotton manufacturing in the southern states, where labour laws permit night operations and the employment of women and children in night work, where wages are very considerably below the wages paid in New England and far below those paid in the Quebec cotton mills, and where mills are operating on mass production on standardized lines, the record of the past few years, and particularly at the present time, is one of non-margin profits. Cotton goods for export are sacrificed and sold to Canadian importers below the cost of production in

The Budget-Mr. Cahan
order to relieve the domestic markets in the United States. Much of this $17,000,000 worth of cotton goods which were imported into Canada from the United States last year came from southern mills and were manufactured and sold under the conditions which I have stated and which would not be tolerated in the province of Quebec or in any other province.
