speechtext: May I ask a question?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will talk to the hon.
gentleman when we come to discuss these items in committee, but as I have only a few minutes at my disposal I should like to proceed without answering questions.
In fact, the competition of imports into Canada of cotton manufactures from the United States is even more of a menace to the cotton industry of this country, and of the province of Quebec in particular, than the competition from Lancashire. Whereas the Canadian tariff rates which are now in force on imports of cotton goods from the United States are only 22^ per cent on grey goods, 25 per cent on white goods, 27 per cent on prints and 30 per cent on coloured goods, the new United States tariff on imports of cotton goods, with a duty of seven cents per pound on raw cotton, will be as follows:
Grey goods: not exceeding No. 90's in quality, 10 per cent ad valorem, and, in addition thereto, for each number, 2%ooths of one per cent ad valorem; exceeding No. 90, 41^ per cent ad valorem. That is, the duty on 20's quality cloth will be 17 per cent and on 40's quality, 24 per cent ad valorem.
White goods: 13 per cent and 3%ooths up to 90's, and exceeding 90's, 44^ per cent ad valorem. That is, the duty on 20's will be 20 per cent and on 40's quality, 27 per cent.
Print and coloured goods: 16 per cent and 3%ooths up to 90's, and exceeding 90's, 47-| per cent ad valorem. That is, the duty on 30's will be 26i per cent, on 40's, 30 per cent, and on 60's, 37 per cent. These are the United States duties which are about to be imposed by their new tariff schedule.
Here is an oportunity staring the Minister of Finance in the face for the imposition of countervailing duties on products on which there are really substantial importations from the United States and which are proving a serious menace to Canadian production and to the employment of Canadian labour. If the government approves the policy of enacting countervailing duties in Canada against increases in the customs duties of the United States, what reasonable grounds can be advanced for their complete failure to protect Canadian cotton mills and their employees against the disastrous competition of the mills
of the southern states? Why should a long established Canadian industry such as the textile industry be sacrificed, throwing thousands of Canadians out of employment and destroying millions of invested capital as they are being destroyed throughout Canada?
The Minister of Finance has turned a blind eye and a deaf ear towards all imports from the United States where countervailing Canadian duties would largely increase remunerative employment in Canada and conserve Canadian capital. Moreover, the drawback provisions of the existing cotton schedules in Canada reduce the real protection of the Canadian cotton mills to a mere shadow of what it purports to be. While the United States converter must place his order for a minimum of 7,500 yards of any particular pattern and pay for the expensive copper rolls, a Canadian converter can place his order with the same United States print works for as little as 2,500 yards of a pattern and, as the copper rolls have already been paid for, this cost is deleted from the price for export to Canada, so that the goods are actually sold in Canada at a less price than that at which they can be purchased by converters in the United States. Canadian mills owing to our situation have to demand a minimum yardage of 3,600 yards and absorb therein the cost of the rolls, although the number of patterns necessarily required to be made by the Canadian print works is very much larger than is made by the average print works in the United States. Obviously the competition of United States prints in this market has become excessively keen and of the most menacing and destructive character.
For export to Canada the American manufacturer makes especially low prices for special lots. He sacrifices in the Canadian market his surplus stocks and substandards of seconds. These goods are offered for export to large Canadian buyers at ridiculously low prices, often below the current American prices of the cotton yarns from which the goods are made, without adding the cost of manufacture and profit. There might be some economic advantage, it will be said, in the importation from the United States of these goods at low prices if the savings thus made were passed on to the Canadian consumer. But such is never the case. The goods are purchased by jobbers in Canada and sold through them to the consumers in this country on the basis of the competitive values of Canadian-made goods, and the actual consumer reaps no advantage whatsoever, while Canadian employees are put out of their employment.
No Canadian industry has recorded a more convincing case for upward tariff revision than
20SS
The Budget-Mr. Cahan

the woollen and worsted cloth manufacturers have done in their several hearings before the tariff board. This was virtually admitted by the government in 1928 when the tariff on imports of wool yarns for weaving purposes from the United Kingdom was removed. The duty of 12^ per cent on wool yarns was removed, and this permitted worsted cloth manufacturers to buy their yarns in England on the same basis as English manufacturers, and at the same time the duty of 24J per cent on imports of cloth was retained, and thus indirectly their net protection was increased. But this was done at the expense of the worsted yarn spinners in this country. Old established and completely equipped mills with wool preparing, carding, combing, drawing and spinning equipment were sacrificed ruthlessly. The wool growing industry in Canada received a set-back, and this government's new tariff policy in 1928 permitted the importation of wool and worsted yarns duty free to displace Canadian-grown wools in the manufacture of cloth from such yarns.
The woollen cloth industry has not benefited because of the technical difficulties connected with the importation of woollen yarns, and because of the fact that all the Canadian woollen mills are completely equipped for the handling and manufacture of wool from the raw state to the finished product, as is the case the world over. Yet, the whole tendency of this government's policy is to lessen the domestic consumption of Canadian-grown wools and to discourage wool production in Canada, a branch of the farming industry for which all admit there are great possibilities in every province in the Dominion, and particularly in the provinces of Quebec and Alberta, where some of the finest clothing and worsted combing wools in the world are now being grown. Wool production on Quebec farms and wool manufacturing in the home and in the factory has been peculiarly a French Canadian industry, but where once there were many flourishing manufacturing plants in the province of Quebec, there are now only three or four cloth mills struggling for existence. The industry has been sacrificed by the existing British preference, and the province of Quebec has been one of the principal losers.
On the other hand, the Canadian market is now being flooded with the very cheapest and lowest quality of woollens that can be manufactured in English, Italian and Czechoslovakian mills. Much of this cloth is entirely unsuited for Canadian climatic conditions. It is made from old rags and muck gathered from the four corners of the globe, 
and its production was intended originally for the low-paid, pauperized populations of. Russia, middle Europe, and Asia. It is cheap,' mungo and shoddy material without'warmth-or wearing quality, but it is showy and it is1 foisted by the thousands of yards upon the' Canadian market to supply Canadian women1 and children and workingmen as a substitute' for the good-wearing, high quality woollens made in Canadian mills or formerly imported from England. Of course, some good high quality woollens are still imported from English and Scottish mills, But the large proportion of importations of woollen cloth intb' Canada at the present time is this low gride' shoddy material, worthless for wear under the' climatic conditions which prevail in this country.	' - '[DOT]
Special treaties with these European countries have been responsible in large measure' for the regrettable conditions in which our' mills is placed. To-day Canadian woollen cloth mills, the few that still remain, are operating only 3 to 4 days a week,' with greatly reduced staffs.
Although wages in English mills are less than 60 per cent of the wages paid in Cana- ' dian woollen mills in the province of Quebec, wages in France, Italy and other European countries are 25 to 50 per cent lower than in Lancashire, England. English woollen and worsted manufacturers have made repeated requests to the British board of trade for a tariff of 33i per cent on imports of wool fabrics into the United Kingdom. This increase was reported upon favourably by the board of trade committee, but it has not yet been acted upon, owing to the change in the British government shortly after the report was brought down. Yet Canada gives to these shoddy products preferential treatment in our own market over the Canadian' product under special treaties which we have negotiated with such countries as France,' Italy and Czechoslovakia.
The destruction of the woollen manufacturing industry in Canada has been a blot on the political administration of this country. To-day, the industry is operating far below the economic minimum. If it is wiped out entirely, or indeed if immediate tariff action is not taken to resuscitate it, British and foreign mills will shortly control this market for woollen goods absolutely. To-day the cost of production in Canada is the price basis, but once "ptoduotion in Canada is removed, this market will be at the mercy of foreign manufacturers, a situation that is, or should be, inconceivable in a country such as Canada, where wool clothing is such an ab-

The Budget-Mr. Cahan
solute necessity and the development of manufacturing industry an economic necessity.	.	.
Development of the silk manufacturing industry in Canada has also been a feature of our industrial expansion during the past few years. The relatively high value of the raw material and the increase in popular demand for silk have been responsible. The high value yields a relatively higher tariff protection on labour cost than is the case with cotton or wool. Moreover, goods containing silk are something of a luxury or are in the luxury class. Development of the silk industry in the province of Quebec has been an outstanding feature of industrial expansion in that province during the past few years.
Now, the government has taken a slap at the silk industry by excluding the excise tax in force in Japan from being reckoned in the cost for duty purposes on silk goods imported into Canada from Japan. When a few years ago Japan imposed the excise tax of 10 per cent on silk manufactures, the Canadian dumping act was enforced and an additional duty of 10 peT cent has since been levied on imports of silk goods from Japan. But now this excise tax will be exempted for duty purposes on imports from Japan.
This exemption seriously affects the silk mills of this country. The development of the industry in Quebec has been due in no small measure to the decrease in Japanese competition induced by this additional 10 per cent duty. It has resulted in several million yards increase in Canadian production of silk fabrics. The exclusion of this excise tax from the cost on which the duty is .to be reckoned is now causing silk manufacturers considerable alarm.
The whole basis of consideration of the textile tariffs by the present government has been wrongly conceived. The incidence of the textile tariffs on the consumer's dollar has been misinterpreted and misunderstood. It is relatively insignificant. Only about 50 per cent of the domestic market for textile fabrics and materials is supplied by Canadian mills. Given a larger share of this market, under an adequate and scientific tariff adjustment, production costs in Canada can 'be decreased, thousands more of Canadian workers can be given employment, and millions of dollars more can be paid out annually in wages. The cost of production of textiles in Canada is the basis of prices for textiles in this market, so that an increased production will inevitably bring about a lowering of prices to the Canadian consumer.
I am not advocating-I have never advocated-that Canadian consumers should pay dividends upon watered stock. The capitalization of existing cotton and woollen mills is not in excess of the value of their assets. If there is such an excess, it can readily be ascertained by the government, who should apply the remedy. I am not advocating-I have never advocated-that customs duties should be invoked to sustain a business which is not thoroughly equipped and efficiently managed. The mills of Canada are well equipped and their management is as competent and as efficient as in the United States or in England. Nor should dividends be declared upon a capitalization which is excessive for the real requirement of the business. I am advocating an honest, efficient administration of the mills; but I am advocating also that the government and parliament of this country should protect our labourers against the cheap labour of Italy, Czechoslovakia, Belgium, and even France, not to speak of Lancashire and the southern states.
But we of the province of Quebec-I have not a dollar in this industry; I am speaking of public opinion-do resent pernicious propaganda, based on misinformation and misunderstanding, which has a tendency to destroy one of the great industries of the eastern provinces of Canada, an industry which we are as competent to administer and maintain as the cotton and woollen manufacturers of the United States or of Great Britain, of Belgium, Italy or Czechoslovakia.
Of course, there are highly specialized products-luxury products-of cotton, silk, and wool, for which there is not sufficient demand in Canada at present to justify the equipment of our mills for their manufacture. These we must continue to import from abroad, and in respect of this branch of the trade we would willingly give the United Kingdom a preference over the United States producers. But it is an economic crime to give to the producers of cottons and woollens in the United States, or even to the producers of Great Britain, a preference over our own workmen, in the markets of our own country.
Some of these industries are now being maintained on the verge of 'bankruptcy by reason of the preferences which prevail in Canada in favour of Great Britain, and also in favour of certain continental countries of Europe, which have hitherto been granted special privileges under existing trade treaties.
Complaint is made that we do not offer constructive policies. I should like to suggest that the duties prevailing on cotton goods
The Budget-Mr. McPhee

prior to February 1928, should be restored forthwith, and this, although it would increase the tariff protection by two and one half per cent, would give employment to several thousands of workmen throughout Canada, including some few thousand workmen and workwomen in the province of Quebec, and would stop the sacrifice and destruction of capital to the extent of a million dollars a year which is now taking place in the cotton and woollen mills of eastern Canada.
I see my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I shall have to take advantage of some other opportunity during this discussion to present a few more suggestions which I should like to make to the house and to the government.

Will my hon. friend now say that in the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, over the opposition of my hon. friends, the government of this country has lost the confidence of the people of Canada? Just in that connection it might be of interest to the house to read an interview with Mr. Clarence Graham, honorary president of the "On-to-the-Bay " Association, which appeared in the press just a few days ago. The interview is as follows:
Mr. Graham estimated that within ten years of the opening of the Hudson Bay route in 1931 there will be at least fifteen million people between the Great lakes and the Pacific ocean.
The British preference, put in a nutshell, simply meant favoured treatment for Britain. In the past there had been a great deal of talk of what had been called "the American penetration of Canada." British preference would be practically a subsidy on goods coming from Britain. Pointing to the advantage in distance of the new route, Mr. Graham stated that Churchill was slightly nearer to Liverpool than New York city, being 2,926 miles compared with slightly more than 3,000 to the latter place. He intimated that opening of the Hudson bay in conjunction with British preference would create such a condition of prosperity on the prairies as would excite a desire south of the border to participate on a par with those living this side of the line.
Is it, then, with regard to our increased trade that the government has lost the confidence of the people of this country? Consult the public statements of every provincial premier throughout Canada, of every bank president, of the presidents of large mercantile concerns. They all testify to the general prosperity of Canada. Just a few days ago I happened to pick up a blotter which has been broadcast throughout Canada by one of the large mercantile concerns of the west. On the back of the blotter appears some interesting data, as follows:
The Budget-Mr. McPhee

Canada's Great Export Growth
The story of Canada as a trading nation in the years since the war is an amazing record of achievement not yet fully recognized by Canadians themselves. Her external trade is now running over three billion dollars a year, compared with two billions only ten years ago.
Most amazing of all has been the growth and variety of Canadian exports. At the beginning of the century, the Dominion was a small country best known for its exports of good wheat. Industrially she was unimportant; a poor crop year made Canada sink into insignificance among the trading nations of the world. All that has been changed. On a per capita basis Canada now stands second among the exporting countries of the world. In 1913, she stood only seventh. But Canadian exports to-day are not all wheat, though wheat remains the backbone of her trading strength. In manufactures alone, Canada still stands second in the world on a per capita basis, exceeded only by Great Britain. Since 1922, Canada has increased its industrial production from $2,500,000,000 to $4,000,000,000. No country in the world has exceeded this rate of growth. . . The record is one which reflects the Dominion's prosperity, and Canadians have a right to feel proud of it.
Is it in the matter of the leadership of the Liberal party that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition says we have lost the confidence of the people of this country? I will let one of the principal Tory papers of Canada answer that question. The Winnipeg Tribune, in its issue of November 1 last, had this to say with reference to the leader of the present government:
Either by good fortune or good management -his opponents say one, his supporters the other-the country at present is both tranquil and prosperous. Really acute political issues are lacking, and such issues as do exist are discussed in calmness and moderation. This fact alone in no slight tribute to the qualities Mr. King brings to his task of leadership.
How, then, do our hon. friends opposite claim that this government has lost the confidence of the people? Some of them refer to the tariff; others say that the Liberal party has stolen the clothes of the Conservative party, and in that contention they are supported to a certain extent by their allies in the southeast corner. When did the British preference ever become a part of the Tory program, in this country? It was first inaugurated by Laurier and Fielding in 1897. If one wants to know the Tory reaction to the inauguration of the British preference in 1897 he only has to read in Hansard of that year the speeches delivered by the Conservative stalwarts of that time. It will be sufficient for me to quote the words of Sir Charles Tupper, who at that time was the leader of the Conservative party. Speaking in the house on April 26, 1897, with regard to the British preference inaugurated by the

Fielding tariff of that year, Sir Charles Tupper
said:
Now, what is the result? The result is that this tariff goes into operation, and the hon. gentleman knows that the industries of this country are already paralyzed in consequence. While hon. members gloat, vindictively gloat, over the destruction of Canadian industries, I was reading the wail, the sorrowful wail, of those industries in the Montreal Gazette, where one manufacturer after another declared that their industries were ruined, that their mills must close, and that they saw staring them in the face a return to the deplorable state of things that existed when the hon. gentleman who last addressed the house was in charge of the fiscal policy of this country. I say that a deeper wrong was never inflicted upon Canada.
Does that look as though the British preference was ever a part of the Tory program? Continuing, Sir Charles Tupper said:
I deplore from the bottom of my heart the ruin that is going to be inflicted upon the best interests of Canada, and upon its great industries. Still, I unhesitatingly say that from a party point of view the hon. gentlemen are doing our work; they are showing the people of this country that no reliance can be placed upon the most solemn declarations that they make, either in the house or out of it; they-are showing the people of this country that, having obtained power, which was ail they wished for, they are now prepared to abuse that power at the cost of the sacrifice of thq industries of Canada.
How similar that seems to be to the language used by the hon. gentlemen opposite.

The tariff has to be readjusted from time to time to bring it into harmony with changed conditions. It has to be readjusted periodically because after the lapse *of a certain period we know that changes in conditions have taken place, and the tariff has to be readjusted in order to correct errors and to remove evil where evil exists.
That is the policy of the Liberal party as enunciated by the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier and which has been repeated throughout Canada over and over again by Liberals of to-day. My hon. friends opposite, assisted by some of their allies to their left, have made the statement that there is very little difference between the Liberal and Conservative parties in regard to the matter of tariff. However, an editorial which appeared in the Manitoba Free Press only a few days ago clears the atmosphere and defines the issue as between the two parties. This editorial, which I think should be on record, reads as follows:
The Issue of the Tariff
Mr. Bennett's attack upon the Liberal tariff was in the true Conservative tradition. Since the Fielding tariff of 1897 Conservatives in attack have never allowed any undue regard for consistency to cramp their style. They have exercised the right to denounce Liberal-made tariffs as a hypocritical betrayal of the supporters of the Liberal government responsible because of the presence in it of provisions patently protectionist. They have also consistently and systematically attacked these tariffs on the ground that they do not supply "adequate protection." In parts of Canada where there is well-defined low-tariff sentiment they have said that there is no tariff issue because both parties are equally protectionist, with sometime the variation that the Conservatives are in reality the true low tariff party. This last line of argument is, however, usually left to confederates, who operate behind a screen-like Milton N. Campbell, the supposedly Progressive M.P. for Mackenzie, who has been busying himself lately in trying to make the people of Saskatchewan believe that their hope for tariff reduction lies in the return to power of Mr. Bennett.
The editorial continues:
But we do not think that now, or at any time in the last thirty years, it has been in the least difficult for an intelligent person to come to an informed opinion as to what the Liberal tariff policy is. It does not favour free trade; it is not primarily concerned with revenue; it does believe in permitting importations under competitive tariff conditions. We should say that it would be a fair definition to state that the Liberals support a competitive tariff policy, while the Conservatives favour a protective tariff looking towards prohibitive rates. The resultant Liberal tariff can only be regarded as low in comparison with protectionist tariffs: it is, in fact, pretty high. But it is now, and has been for 30 years, much lower than any possible alternative Conservative tariff; and there never was a time when the divergence in policy was more marked than it is right now.
The issue in the coming election is the tariff. The choice is between a moderate tariff which permits us to take pay for our exports in the
The Budget-Mr. McPhee

form of imports, and a high tariff intended to prohibit imports and hamper that foreign trade which is the very life-blood of western Canada. The electors of western Canada will have to line up on this issue, for or against a policy of tariff exclusion.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been customary for the present government during its regime which has existed almost continuously, from the beginning of 1922 to the present, to enlarge in the speech from the throne and also in the budget speech on the prosperity which Canada, it claims, is enjoying under its leadership. This year has been no exception to the rule. The government has both in the speech from the throne and in the budget speech claimed prosperity. I propose to consider some of these claims, not year by year, but rather in the light of experience of the years during which the governmefft has been in office.
Agriculture has always been regarded as one of the basic industries of the country. Early in the session several discussions took place on the various phases of agriculture and it was demonstrated in the debates that that basic industry was in a condition not at all in keeping with the claims made in the budget. Conclusive evidence of this is found in a circular letter sent out under the signature of the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. This letter, which is in part, as follows, refers to only a few branches of the agricultural industry:
You are, I understand, interested in live stock of some kind, and are therefore, I have no doubt, interested in Canada's holding her place, and even doing a little better than that on the world's markets for various live stock products. Now, as a matter of fact, Canada seems unfortunately to be losing ground in this connection. For instance, we no longer export any-eggs or butter; we send abroad very little dressed poultry or lamb; our exports of beef cattle are dwindling; our shipments of beef are decreasing; our shipments of bacon, which a few years ago ivere very large, have almost disappeared, and our shipments of cheese are

The Budget-Mr. White (London)
rapidly falling off	Such trade is essential
we believe if our farmers are to hope to do more than eke out a bare living on the land.
That is a most damaging confession, and now that the government have been eight years in office it would be interesting to have the replies that are sent to their query. We can, however, give the departmental officials credit for being alive to the danger and for trying to find a remedy.
In former days we -used to market a great deal of our farm produce in the United States. If we look back over the records of trade we shall find there have been some very serious changes and also the reasons for the drop in trade so far as that country is concerned. The Commercial Intelligence Journal periodically prints a record of the exports, from
Canada to the United States, of the principal commodities produced on Canadian farms or manufactured directly from such farm products. In the issue showing the report of the last six months ending March, 1930, we find a startling record as to the result of our business with our neighbours to the south, and also the reasons therefor. We find that in the six months ended March, 1921, we had supplied the United States market with farm product to the value of $130,517,000 and that during the six months ended March, 1930, our exports of farm products to the United States had dropped to $24,645,000. The reason for that is to be found in the records of the United States tariff rates. Their rates in 1921 and to-day are as follows:

Those duties have had the result of causing a depreciation in our trade in the American market of eighty per cent.
What did this government do when the Fordnev-McCumber tariff of September, 1922, came into force? For one thing, they evolved 1he Petersen contract. For a second thing, they looked for wider markets. Third, they tried to reduce the cost of implements of production. Fourth, they lowered tariffs. Now, after eight years in office, when the government is faced with a further increase in American duties, it brings down countervailing duties. If countervailing duties is the right policy now, it was the right policy in 1922, when the Fordney-McCumber tariff became law. But in spite of the urging of the opposition, the government accepted the situation in 1922 without a protest, and the consequence is that our trade in the American market suffered a reduction of eighty per cent. Now, when the balance of our trade in that market is threatened, the government are moving to save the remaining twenty per cent by countervailing duties. The time to apply
remedial measures was when the greatest damage was being done in 1923.
We all know what happened to the Petersen contract, the government's first reply to the Fordney-McCumber tariff. It is not necessary to enlarge upon that, or upon the object of the Petersen contract or upon what happened to it when it was considered by a committee of this house.
The search for wider markets resulted in many treaties being made, one of which was the French treaty, the dire results of which have been explained to this house on more than one occasion. Then there was the trade agreement with New Zealand. This was under discussion in the house very recently, when the government defended the New Zealand trade agreement in spite of the large importations of New Zealand butter, mutton and other products that are coming into Canada from that country. In the month of March of this year the government defended it as being a splendid agreement, and then in the month of April they gave notice of its termination, driven to it, no doubt, by the activities of the Conservative opposition. In the meantime the government have been bombarded b3r requests and complaints from the fruit growers, the vegetable growers, the tobacco growers, the sheep raisers and the producers of dairjr products, and the results of the government's efforts on their behalf we find in the present budget.

The Budget-Mr. White (London)
As to cheaper implements of production, the budget of 1924 reduced the duties on agricultural implements and machinery. Many items were reduced, the reductions varying from five per cent up to twelve and one-half per cent. Members of the government have made great claims as to the reductions that have been made in the price to the consumer as a consequence of these reductions in the *duties on agricultural implements. In spite of that, the importations of agricultural implements have largely increased.
I wish to pass to a consideration of the effect of the volume of this manufacturing business so far as Canada is concerned. The Bureau of Statistics has issued a bulletin covering the agricultural implement industry in Canada in 1928, and it contains the statement that during 1928 more , money was spent in Canada on agricultural implements and machinery than in the preceding year. It goes on to state that this increase in demand for farm implements was largely supplied by imported goods, as lower levels of production were reported for Canadian-made products. Production values dropped in 1928, while imports advanced in the same year. According ;o the figures given in this bulletin, the apparent consumption of agricultural implements in Canada rose to $66,000,000 in 1928 as compared with $52,000,000 in 1927.
The percentage of Canadian-made implements bought by the Canadian consumer is of great interest. I find from the Bureau of

Statistics that in 1923, the year before the great reduction in the duties on agricultural implements, Canada produced 70 per cent of her requirements and purchased 30 per cent. These figures have been practically reversed. In 1925, one year after the reduction in duty, Canada produced 67 per cent and bought 33 per cent; in 1926 she produced 55 per cent and bought, largely from the United States, 45 per cent; in 1927 the figures stand 50-50; in 1928, the last year for which figures are complete, Canada produced only 40 per cent and purchased 60 per cent, almost entirely from the United States. This is a damaging statement so far as the agricultural implement industry of Canada is concerned.
A few days ago the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) delivered an address in Woodstock, and on the platform supporting him were the representatives of the federal ridings of North Oxford (Mr. Allan) and South Oxford (Mr. Cayley). They lauded the Minister of Finance and his budget. I wonder if the Minister of Justice knew that within shouting distance of the platform on which he was making his speech there existed a wagon factory which had been closed within the last three months? That factory did a good business for twenty-five years, it increased its operations, and it not only made farm wagons, but also freight wagons and sleighs and children's wagons. The firm ceased operations

The Budget-Mr. White (London)
three months ago and is now bankrupt. There is no doubt in my mind that the failure has been brought about by the reduction of the duties on agricultural implements made in 1924, because the duty on wagons at that time was reduced from seventeen and a half, general tariff, to ten per cent. What message of cheer did the Minister of Justice bring to the shareholders in that defunct institution? What message of encouragement did he bring to the workmen who had lost their jobs in that factory? He said, in effect, as he extolled the present government:	We know you are
out of a job, but farm wagons, on which the British preferential duty has been five per cent, we will admit free; freight wagons, on which the British preferential duty has been seventeen and a half per cent, we will also admit free; as to children's wagons, we will reduce the general rate from thirty-five to thirty per cent, the intermediate from thirty to twenty-five per cent, and we will make the British preference ten per cent instead of twenty-two and a half per cent. That, sir, is comparable in its heartlessness with the statement of the Prime Minister only a short time ago in which he dealt with the unemployment situation in the provinces under Conservative government. What recourse has the wagon company? None. All it can do is console itself with the ancient promise of the Prime Minister that " no legitimate company making a legitimate profit need fear any action on the part of the Liberal government." The futility of it all is that our manufacturing establishments are being put out of business and the price of wagons is no lower.
I am of the opinion, and this opinion is based on forty years' experience in manufacturing in the metal industry, that with the market we have in Canada assured to our manufacturers of implements by a reasonable tariff, they could on account of mass production make and sell implements at a much lower price than obtains to-day. It may be urged that prices will soar. They did not in 1922. Now we have a tariff board with a staff of men claimed to be experts. They have visited the plants where these implements are manufactured, and they should know the cost of production. If they do not, how can they arrive at the proper customs duty to apply to each of these items? If they know the cost of production they ought to know if prices are exorbitant, and if this is the case they should apply the remedy without any difficulty.
It has been said that since the duties on agricultural implements have been lowered more men are being employed in the industry than formerly. That statement may be true, 2419-133
but the percentage of implements made in Canada has fallen from seventy per cent in 1923 to forty per cent in 1928. If we had the seventy per cent production which we enjoyed in 1923, instead of having ten or eleven thousand men employed in the industry to-day we might be employing twenty thousand, and they would be getting steady work instead of looking for jobs.
When this so-called reduction in the cost of the implements of production was attempted by a reduction in the customs tariff it was accompanied by a reduction in duty on the raw materials which are used in the manufacture of these implements. Pig iron was placed on the free list, and in 1928 we imported 8.392 tons; castings were placed on the free list, and we imported in that year $345,000 worth; rolled iron and steel were also placed on the free list, and we imported in that year sixty-seven thousand tons; on another item under the heading of "other iron and steel products" which includes nuts, bolts, and other articles entering into the manufacture of these implements, the duty was reduced to six per cent, and in 1928 we imported these articles from the United States to the value of $4,321,000. The net result to the primary operations in iron and steel is that we have been producing less than we did in 1913, the year before the war.
I have under my hand Iron and Steel and Their Products in Canada in 1927, a publication issued under the authority of the hon. James Malcolm, Minister of Trade and Commerce. It deals with the production of pig iron, and on page 62 will be found a report of Canada's production in the years since 1913 up to the present time. In 1913 we produced over
1,000,000 tons of pig iron; from 1922 to 1927, the years when this government was in power, we produced an average of 649,000 tons annually, or only sixty-four per cent of what we produced in 1913. On page 63 the capacity of the blast furnaces in Canada is given. Their capacity is stated to be from 1,000,000 to 1,-
500,000	tons a year; in 1927 we produced only
649,000	tons. That will give the house some idea how these establishments are running on short time or are closed for a large portion of the year.
The manufacturers of iron and steel, of course, have been dissatisfied with this condition of affairs, and ever since 1926 the Minister of Finance has been importuned by many of them to reclassify the iron and steel schedules, and at last we have such a reclassification in this budget. Although the primary producers were sacrificed in 1924, six years later the Minister of Finance tells this house that

The Budget-Mr. While (London)
the object of his budget is to help the primary producers of iron and steel. He is supported in that statement by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), who spoke a few days ago along the same lines. In this budget there have been many changes in the duties, notably in the British preference, the object being "to trade with those who are willing to trade with us."
It is difficult to estimate the effects of the budget, but we do know that Canadian manufacturers are now being undersold in many lines by United States producers, and we do know that if Britain expands her trade she will have at least to equal, if not underbid the United States prices. It is a question whether equal prices will turn our trade to England, because geographical position has to be considered; there is the matter of the suitability of American goods as compared to English goods. Then there is the matter of the ease with which differences between buyer and seller can be adjusted. All these matters will militate against the importation of British goods, and if British goods do come in they will come in at the expense of Canadian labour. It must be remembered that every ton of goods imported, no matter where from, means that one ton less is made in Canadian factories by Canadian workmen. The government has had a change of heart in the matter of applying duties. It evidently now believes in the brick for brick policy which was condemned by them on almost every political platform in this country during the 1926 election campaign. They have, adopted that policy, if we may judge from the budget,and they now say it is a good policy for the grain growers; I wonder if the government believes that it is a good policy for the manufacturers. If so, they have not practised it.
There are some anomalies in the present iron and steel schedule. The first item in that schedule is the one regarding scrap iron and steel. Formerly those products carried a duty of 50 cents per ton, but now they are free. I wonder if the tariff board or the Minister of Finance have made any inquiry as to the position as far as scrap iron is concerned. If they had made an inquiry they would have found that the material mentioned in section (a) of item 373, which is wrought scrap and is now on the free list, was imported into Canada in the last five years to the extent of 40.000 tons; it was exported however to the extent of 378,000 tons. There is no record during the last five years in which the exports do not exceed the imports. Under those conditions the item of wrought scrap

iron on the free list will have very little effect. It is considered to be good practice in the operation of open hearth furnaces to use a considerable quantity of scrap; this use of wrought scrap does not interfere with the production of pig iron. The scrap is used in almost equal quantities with the pig iron in the interests of economy and good furnace performance.
The next item under the same heading is cast iron scrap. This is one type of scrap which interferes with the production of pig iron. The duty on pig iron is now $2.50 whereas cast iron scrap is free. The importation of this scrap cast iron means just so much less pig iron to be supplied from Canadian furnaces; the free entry will probably increase the importation of this particular item. In the year 1928 we imported 9,900 tons.
Another item in the scrap schedules is that of railway rails. The articles referred to are used rails brought into the country for rerolling and to be made into other forms of rolled bars, such as concrete reinforcement. The item of railway rails is one which comes into direct competition with the production of pig iron and the primary production of steel. In the last five years we have imported
366,000	tons. The government has raised the duty on billets by $2, and it encourages the importation of old rails to compete with the billets from which bars are made.
Take the items of blooms, cogged ingots, slabs and billets. In 1928 we imported 44,000 tons of this material. In the same year Canada produced 778,000 tons of billets, or 95 per cent of her total requirements. It will be apparent to hon. members that 44,000 tons represents only 5 per cent of our requirements. In the same year there were imported 127,600 tons of old rails to compete with Canadian billets, and these billets are used to make almost the same quality of bars as the old rails. It will be apparent to hon. members that the importation of old rails has a direct bearing on the reduction in the quantity of steel produced, although the government seem to be under the impression that the addition of $2 per ton on billets will make a difference.
Mr. 'CANTLEY:	It is replaced with material of a poorer quality.

speechtext:
As the hon.
member for Pictou has said-and he has spent a lifetime in the business-it is replaced with material of a poorer quality. In connection with the hot rolled bars and rods there is a worse situation; the duty remains the same. In 1927 Canadian mills sold 190,000 tons of this particular material. In the same year we imported 118,000 tons; last year the

The Budget-Mr. Denis
amount was 173,000 tons. In other words, Canada imported 40 per cent of her consumption in rolled iron and steel while her rolling mill equipment has not been fully operative. To my mind such action is not aiding a primary industry. To raise the duty on ingots in order to protect 5 per cent of our requirements and to neglect the duty on bars when 40 per cent are being imported is not the way to help a primary industry.
I regret that I have not time to go into further detail in connection with the iron and steel schedule. All I can say is that there are some items which appear to encourage the manufacture of steel in Canada. The extra duty on alloy steels is one of them. The matter of heavy structural steel is dependent on an order in council, and it strikes me that any maunfacturing concern which will spend a million dollars or a million and a half for the construction of a heavy structural mill is taking great chances and is "putting its trust in princes" when it relies for its returns on an order in council which will impose a certain duty. On medium structural steel the duty has been doubled. The duty on plates has been increased, and this increase will probably result in further manufacturing in Canada. There will not be much change in regard to sheets. American producers do not seem to worry about the situation. The Canadian Steel Corporation, Limited, at Ojibway, has refused to be hurried as far as construction is concerned. While its plant has been under construction for several years there seems to be no probability of its entering the market immediately, so far as the production of primary steel is concerned.
Taking the whole- history of the government we find that there has been damage to agriculture. An attempt to reduce the cost of the implements of production has failed. There has been damage to the iron and steel and textile industries. Any prosperity which Canada enjoys in regard to industries is not by reason of any help which the government has given, but rather in spite of it. This proposed revision of the tariff is a mere patchwork; it puts up a little here and takes off a little there; it helps someone at this end of the country and hinders someone at the other end. To my mind what Canada needs is proper consideration of her primary industries and the adoption of tariff schedules which will foster the preliminary stages of our basic industries. After that is done consideration may be given to the secondary processes and so on until all industry has an equal opportunity to develop and to give employment to our people. The present budget does not measure up to that need, and I propose to vote against it.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must first offer my
congratulations to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the government for having chosen the Hon. Mr. Dunning as Minister of Finance. I do not think that a better choice could have been made.
A few days ago, the hon. Minister of Finance brought down in the house his first budget and submitted to us the financial, economic and trade situation of this country. Notwithstanding that the hon. minister did not comply with the definition of the dictionary, as he was reproached for, he nevertheless told us that our country, under the present administration, continued its ascending march towards progress and prosperity. Our national debt which, under the Conservative rule, increased by leaps and bounds, was reduced by $80,000,000 during this fiscal year, and by $257,800,000, within the last five years. Our trade with other countries was not as prosperous this year as during the preceding years; we registered an unfavourable balance of $103,000,000. This is due to the fact that the wheat pool in the west, either rightly or wrongly, refused to sell their wheat at the price fixed by the dealers in London. This slight disappointment can only be momentary. Already, since the opening of navigation we have noticed that our wheat shipments have been larger than at this period, last year. In regard to the fiscal year ending on March 31, 1930, the statement of the hon. Minister of Finance shows a surplus of more than $44,000,000, this has helped to reduce our national debt. The receipts amounted to $447,322,000, showing a slight reduction of $14,325,000 as compared with that of the preceding year. This decrease must not astonish us, considering the reductions in taxation effected last year, and which were estimated at more than $25,000,000. The same thing may happen this year owing to the decrease of the sales tax, from 2 to 1 per cent, which it is estimated will amount to $22,000,000. I do not think that there is any one in this house who will reproach this government for having reduced the sales tax, a reduction which was to the advantage of the most numerous and the least wealthy class, the consumers, the majority being workmen. If the manufacturers insist on not paying their employees wages proportionate to their profits and the protection they are given by this government, they will have to settle the matter with that same government. Do you wish another proof of the sympathy of the government towards the workmen? At this present session the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), got this house to adopt a measure obliging all contractors obtaining contracts
The Budget-Mr. Denis

from the government to observe the eight hour day and pay their employees fair and equitable wages. The government desired by this act that the workman, who is the most important factor in all industries, and without whom nothing could be done, should divide in a fair proportion the profits realized. The workman, like all other citizens, must live and it is but fair that the fruit of his wages should give him sufficient purchasing powers to buy what he needs for his existence and that of his family. Of what use would it be to the manufacturer to produce, if the workmen had not the necessary money to purchase his products? Inevitably these industries and their owners would face complete failure. The object which this present government has in mind through its tariff policy, is to grant to all and every one the protection to which he has a right without being detrimental to others. No one has a right to get rich at the expense of others. Before the law, we are all equal.
There is another diuty incumbent on the government of any country, which owing to its population, industrial and trade development cannot suffice to itself, if it is to keep up most friendly trade relations with other countries. That is why the government has made certain changes to its tariff schedule. It took no accounts of the theories of protectionist or free traders, 'but rather of the needs of the people and advantages that they might obtain from these tariff changes. Our farmers complained that there existed an unfair competition in butter by New Zealand; the Government asked the tariff commission to make an inquiry, and as a result the tariff was changed so as to do them Justice, by establishing a preferential tariff of * cents per pound. Our truck gardeners also complained of the competition carried on by the United States against their vegetables. Immediately an inquiry was started, and they are glad to hear to-day that the government by its budget has established a tariff which allows them to compete advantageously with the United States products. But we, city representatives, have no desire to see, by this tariff change, our workmen obliged to pay dearer for their commodities. This question was carefully considered by the government and the1 solution arrived at, I am convinced, will satisfy all concerned.
It is unfortunate, however, that Conservative importers, with the sole aim of deceiving public opinion, for election purposes, thought fit to raise the price of their goods, and this without any reason, making their clients believe that the tariff was the cause. It is some of the Tory party's propaganda and

falsehoods: the Canadian people are wise to their tricks and will not allow themselves to be deceived when the time comes to give their verdict, at the next general election. Before resuming my seat, allow me, sir, to draw the attention of the goverment to the request of the postal employees for an increase in salary. I think that this request should be given, further consideration. If it were thought proper to appoint a commission with reference to the increases to be granted to a certain class of employees, I think that the postal workers generally, also deserve that we take an interest in their lot and help them by complying with their request.
There is another question, sir, that I should like to submit to the government. There has been an attempt to introduce in this House a measure tending to make the Canadian people believe that a subsidy for the construction of a national highway would have greatly helped to relieve the unemployment that existed last winter. As representative of the province of Quebec, I have been and I am still apposed to a subsidy for the construction of a highway, so called national. The province of Quebec has always led in the movement to build up good roads. We did not depend on the Dominion government to construct these national highways and I think that the other provinces should have as much pride as the province of Quebec and build their highways without coming to Ottawa to seek the help of the Dominion government. If unemployment, sir, exists, it is not the Dominion government's fault. On the contrary, our government, through the Minister of Labour, did all it could to induce public companies and private firms which had work to be done, to begin as soon as possible, so as to employ those who were in need of work to provide for their families.
After these few comments, I am pleased to state in the house that, as representative of a Montreal riding, the St. Denis constituency, I am proud of the budget presented this year by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and I fed certain that it will 'be given at the next general election the entire approval of the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I very greatly regret that my lack of knowledge of the beautiful language which has just flowed from the lips of my eloquent friend does not permit me to address the house in the same way. No doubt that is my loss; it is the loss of many people in this country, which some day we shall see remedied.

The Budget-Mr. Maloney
It has been my privilege on four or five occasions to say a word in connection with the budgets which have been delivered in this house and, Mr. Speaker, I recall with sorrow that the man whom I have been accustomed to hear deliver the budget speech during the last five years has passed away. The late Minister of Finance, even though we did not on all occasions agree with him politically, was a man whom we trusted absolutely, a man who I believe had the confidence of ninety per cent of our people. To me it is a matter of very great regret indeed that he has passed away and left us forever. His successor is an outstanding citizen who, we were glad to see, was sufficiently strong in health to deliver a budget of a character unusual in the history of our country.
Speaking as an individual member of the opposition, and for myself only, I should like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that under the laws of this country there are several kinds of robbery. There is the ordinary, eveiy day robbery; there is highway robbery, and there is robbery with violence. When we come to consider this budget we find that all three kinds of robbery have been combined, and we can only say that the present Minister of Finance and those associated with him have committed at once all three varieties of this offence. As a matter of fact the only difference between certain hon. gentlemen in Canada and Jesse James is the fact that Jesse James had a horse. Surely when hon. gentlemen opposite endeavour to impress upon the country the attitude they are now taking, they cannot be serious. I will say this to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King): If he can put this budget across, the day after the election he can start out and commit murder whenever he wishes, and he will be surely acquitted.
However, the people of Canada cannot be fooled all the time. Almost every item in the budget presented by the Minister of Finance is something for which we have been fighting for many years. It is a very fine tribute indeed to the great party on this side of the house. I think I am letting you in on no profound secret, Mr. Speaker, when 1 say that when the people of Canada have a chance to pronounce their views, which I hope will be within the next sixty or sixty-five days, they will give to the party which has been endeavouring to propound these policies the opportunity to put them into effect.
The budget will not be the only matter discussed before the people of this country during the next sixty or seventy days. We will discuss t'he record of this government for
the past nine years. Now, on their death bed, they are repenting and endeavouring to adopt the cures which we have been propounding for that length of time, but they will have to answer for their record during that period. To-day, when almost every industry in this country has been, practically ruined, with the farmers almost in penury, the government adopt the policies we have *been advocating for the past nine years.
We must also consider the record of this government in many matters in addition to the fiscal policy; we must consider matters of taxation and of expenditure. Here is a party which stood for low taxation and economy. What have they been practising in the last few years? Even to-day what is their platform on economy? They'are spending $22,000,000 more this year than was spent last year, and yet they say they are trying to save the money of the people of Canada. How are they spending that money? This is what the people will want to know. Are they spending it in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole? Let us consider for a few moments what is happening right here in the city of Ottawa. This is a matter which I have mentioned before and which will be mentioned again; it is of great importance to the whole Dominion of Canada. I refer to the amount of money which this government is prepared to spend in order to destroy perfectly good property in the city of Ottawa. Is that being done in the interests of the hard working farmer and the hard working labourer of this country? This government is prepared to do that, but how could that money have been spent? The proposal was made to the government that instead of destroying perfectly good property it should do something constructive; it should build a highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It should spend millions of dollars upon that work rather- than to tear down good property in this city. If that was done it would mean the employment of many thousands of men throughout Canada and would afford relief to a situation which is inimical to our welfare. This government has known of the unemployment in this country, but it has done absolutely nothing. An opportunity was presented to link the east with the west and at the same time give employment to thousands of our citizens. But the government has taken no action in this respect, and that is an issue which will come before the electors of Canada during the next two or three months.
In addition, there is the expenditure which is being made upon foreign legations. What are those legations doing for Canada? What
The Budget-Mr. Maloney

benefit have they been to the people as a whole? What has our friend Mr. Marler done in Tokyo for the benefit of Canada? How much has he cost the people of this country? What has our friend the Hon. Vincent Massey, in the meantime in Washington cost the people of this country, and of what benefit has he been to Canada? Our idea is to take the money being spent in Washington and Tokyo and spend it in aid of technical education. As you know, Mr. Speaker, our system of education is not one which brings the best out of a boy or a girl. From the time of entering until the time of leaving the common school, our system of education guides the scholar along one certain line, a line leading to the universities. AVe have not forgotten that ninety per cent of our boys and girls never reach the university? AArhen the young people leave the primary or secondary school, after matriculation, they have a knowledge of algebra, a knowledge of English, an imperfect knowledge of French and Latin, and a smattering of other subjects, but what position in life are they able to occupy? They cannot go into a store and keep a set of books; they cannot go on the farm and work the land- they are too highly educated for that. They cannot take up a trade because they have not received the necessary training. Technical education would mean that boys and girls at the tender age of twelve, fourteen or fifteen would have installed into their minds the idea of taking up some profession or calling worth while. But the government says: No, we would rather spend three million dollars on Messrs. Vincent Massey and Herbert Marler than spend one million dollars on the boys and girls of Canada. This is another matter which will come before the electors of Canada, in addition to the notorious highway robbery which I have already mentioned.
Has this government been a friend of the farmer? Consider the condition of agriculture to-day as compared with that of nine years ago. At that time the farmers of Canada were fairly prosperous; they were able to pay their debts and continue to carry on. From end to end of Canada to-day you will find in section after section, farm after farm abandoned. That applies even in the most highly developed portions of our agricultural districts. In the county of Oxford, which is perhaps the garden spot of Canada, there is to-day a smaller agricultural population than there was at the time of confederation. Why should that be? Simply because of the fact that this government during the last nine years has allowed every foreign competitor to dump his farm products into Canada in competition with our
[DOT]'Mr. Maloney.]
own farmers. In the county of Renfrew for the last eight or ten months we have been eating beef and mutton, produced where? Not in Renfrew county, not in Ontario, not in Canada, but in a country seven thousand miles away-that beef and mutton came all the way from New Zealand, and was dumped here in competition with Canadian farmers. How has this happened? This government passed an order in council without the consent of this parliament, without the consent of the people of Canada, which allows these products to enter Canada in unfair competition with our own products. Not only is beef and mutton allowed to enter under these conditions, but millions and millions of pounds of butter are being dumped here in competition with the products of our own farms. Then, the farmer having been ruined, and the dairying industry killed, in order to procure a few votes the government becomes penitent and says: AVe will adopt the policy which our opponents have been advocating.
However, there is one other product which has been forgotten-wool and wool products. Twenty years ago we had in the district from which I come ten or twelve woollen mills, all of which were running full blast day and night. What are the present conditions? Out of those ten or twelve mills, only two are left, and one is making a struggle for existence. The others are closed and locked up tight. AA7hy? Because this government has allowed woollen goods and certain grades of wool to enter free of duty, and we are unable to compete with the outside world. Possibly next year, if by any unfortunate chance the present government should be returned, after this industry is dead and gone it will accept the advice we have been trying to give it, and a tariff reform will be brought into force which will protect the woollen mills of Canada. However, that is carrying the question too far.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let us look at these matters from the point of view of Canada's future. The policy of the party of which I have the honour to be a member is a policy for Canada first, last and always, a policy which means the manufacturing in this country of our own raw products, a policy which will preserve for the people of Canada our own markets against any other nation, no matter which it may be, because our first duty is to. our own people. AVhen the Canadian people within the next few weeks have a chance to pronounce upon this budget, I feel, as I think seventy-five per cent of the electors of this country feel that my honoured leader

The Budget-Mr. Rheaume
will have an opportunity to form a government, and then indeed Canada will enter an era of prosperity

The necessity and urgency of these public improvements insisted on for over 20 years, cannot be gainsaid. On the south side of the Lachine canal, covering a distance of three miles, there is a progressive population which will soon attain the figure of 200,000.

The Budget-Mr. Rheaume
congestion is intolerable in the morning and evening, when the workmen go and come from their work.
If we add to the ordinary traffic of a city which is growing every day as that of Montreal, the traffic of tourists who each year invade the metropolis of Canada, and two-thirds of whom pass over the Wellington bridge or that of Cote St. Paul, the house will have a fair idea of the necessity and urgency of the tunnels requested.
On what grounds would the Dominion government be called upon to contribute to the construction of these tunnels? First, the Dominion government is obliged to help traffic where its canals and railways are operating. When bridges become insufficient, it must provide other means to meet the needs of traffic. In the case under consideration it is proved that only tunnels could remedy the evil of which people complain.
Moreover, navigation will benefit greatly by the construction of those tunnels. Indeed, the vessels which carry our good will gain an appreciable time; the accidents which have occurred at the Lachine canal bridge and interfered with navigation for a few days, would then be a thing of the past.
With the competition that Canada meets over its wheat in the world markets, these advantages to navigation which I have just enumerated, will certainly be appreciated by the members of this house.
Now these improvements, like elections, require something more than prayers. What will be the cost of those tunnels? The engineers who have studied these two schemes have fixed the approximate cost of the tunnel at Wellington street, at $2,500,000, and that of Cote St. Paul, at $2,130,000. The cost seems high, but I shall show that the government will make a good bargain by contributing to them. The plans already prepared include the necessary space for two tramway tracks two vehicular roads, and a sidewalk six feet wide for pedestrians.
Now, sir, how will the cost of construction be distributed? Montreal, which will maintain on its own responsibility, and become the owners of, these tunnels will pay one-third of the work. The Montreal Tramway Company undertakes to pay another third There would only remain for the Dominion government to pay the balance, that is one-third of the cost.
I shall now show that this contribution of the Dominion government would be an advantageous one financially. It will cost the government very little to help in the construction of these tunnels; indeed, the Wellington street bridge was completed in 1898; it is

therefore 32 years old. Thirty-two years in power for a good government like the present one is not much, but for an iron bridge, it is practically the limit of its usefulness. The Cote St. Paul bridge is about as old, perhaps a few years less. It will be necessary to rebuild those two bridges in the near future. What will it cost the country? An amount not less than 8400,000 for each bridge. Add to the cost of construction, the operating and maintenance costs which amounts to about $20,000 per year for each bridge; now, the capitalized value of this yearly expenditure, $20,000 at 5 per cent, amounts to $400,000. The construction, therefore, of the government in the proportion of one-third would represent about the same amount which would be necessary to construct, operate and maintain the two new bridges.
I shall add nothing further, as the end of the session is near. I think, sir, that I have proved my case, as we say in court, and I feel confident that the supplementary estimates will help to solve a problem which interests greatly the city of Montreal and the whole country as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a celebrated English parliamentarian stated that a new member should speak in the house only after having listened attentively during two sessions; that at the third session, he should speak but for ten minutes. I wish to conform, in a large measure to this advice, and I shall restrict myself as much as possible to the time limit indicated.
Before proceeding further, sir, allow me to recall to the hon. members the memory of the late Mr. G. D. Morin, my predecessor. Mr. Morin was highly thought of by his colleagues, friends and all his constituents. He was a hard worker and very devoted to his duties. The country lost a great man; his family, a good father and the county a distinguished member. Mr. Morin was the worthy successor of Mr. J. E. Edmond Marcile, who represented the county of Bagot during twenty-eight years, and his constituents reposed all their confidence in him up to the very last, since they elected him, in 1925, hardly a month before his death. I trust that the example of my predecessors may be a guide to me in my public life.
I took a great interest in the debates of the present session, and I studied as much as it was possible for me to do, the legislation enacted. Allow me, sir, to congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the wise way in which

The Budget-Mr. Dumaine
he leads the Liberal party and directs the destinies of Canada. The right hon. Prime Minister is a great statesman, and has a wide-world reputation. All legislation which he has passed is sound, human and loj-al. I would not be doing my duty and would be unfair to our hon. ministers if I did not give them credit for the good and sound administration of their respective departments. And you, Mr. Speaker, you have my entire admiration and full confidence for the wise way with which you preside over proceedings of this house.
As I wish to be brief, allow me, sir, to say a few words on questions of a general interest to the country and of immediate need to my constituents.
On May 1, the hon, minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) submitted to us the budget for the current year. The reduction of the national debt, as well as that on the income tax and sales tax were highb^ appreciated by all citizens of this country, Conservatives as well as Liberals, and this is vouched by all the newspapers which were published the day following this great event.
This year again, more than any other, the government seemed to take a greater interest in the farming class which I have the honour of representing in the house. The prohibition of United States farm products on our markets is a great help to Canadian fanners. The Americans used to dump the surplus of their products on our markets at ridiculous prices, and they prohibited our products on their own markets. I congratulate the government on the stand they have taken. One must not forget that the farmers belong to the class which is the least organized in this country, and we must protect them.
The farming industry differs from other industries; there are a number of factors which makes its management difficult. The crop is either good or bad, depending upon the weather, and even if the market is favourable, if a farmer has no crop he oanniot sell anything; and vice versa, should the crop be excellent and the market poor, the farmer is often obliged to sell at ridiculous prices even sometimes at 50 per cent of cost price. Yet the owner of a farm is always obliged to pay, each year, his taxes and meet various other payments, and, furthermore, interests at rates often too high.
One of our devoted colleagues, the hon. member for St. John Iberville (Mr. Benoit) introduced a resolution in this house to reduce the rate of interest on farm loans from 61 per cent to 5i per cent. All the members of Quebec and a great number of members from other provinces supported this resolution and signed a request asking the hon. Minister of Finance to reduce by one per cent the rate of interest at present in force.
I trust that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) will grant our request, because I think it just and well founded. If we turn to the other countries which are favoured with a farm loans act, we find that the rate of interest is lower than the one at present in force in this country. I state again that this reduction is necessary and that we should be granted our request.
I should like to see this farm loans act administered by a federal commission, and paid from the -public treasury; that each province which benefits by it should look after the local administration, and that the borrower should -pay but the cost and fees of the examination of titles, acts and registration.
Another essential point to attain the real end for which the Canadian farm loans was established, is that the valuation of properties be made on the actual value of the properties and that the amount of the loan be not less than the f of the estimated value of the property. I am confident, sir, that if we thus assisted the farmers, without too m-uch cost to the country, the farming classes would feel happier and more prosperous.
As the hon. member for Jolette (Mr. Fer-land) stated in his last speech, -the Bankruptcy Act of 1919, caused considerable harm to farmers by allowing them to assign their property. This act, drawn up in terms sufficiently vague as to be interpreted in any way, -makes it possible for certain speculators to roam about the country-side and incite the farmers to assign their property. The latter lose their farms and remain with more debts than they had previously. Money lenders in good faith also lost -their loans owing to the fact of having made such advances during the three months preceding the bankruptcy. This act has been very harmful to the credit of fanners, and to-day, it is a problem for the owner of a farm valued at about $10,000 -to borrow $4,000 or $5,000. These are the reasons why I insist so much that the Canadian farm loans act should become a real help to the farming class.
I would further draw the attention of the government to the estimates for the Department of Agriculture. These estimates are not sufficiently large compared to others of less immediate importance, aviation for instance. Every year the Department is forced to ask for supplementary estimates, and while this is going on, our people are waiting for their money. Within the last few years, the government has wisely taken the initiative of reviving the dairy industry, and, with that
The Budget-Mr. Dumaine

object in view it has established restricted areas. I believe that this Act will be of great help to the farming class, providing that it is well administered. Inspection has already started in my county, and I think that it will be further continued in the autumn. I trust that the government will vote the necessary money to indemnify, as soon as possible, the farmers who may have sustained losses. By indemnifying them within 30 days, the loss sustained will be less felt, and the farmer will be able to renew his herd and get immediate results.
I am pleased-although I expected it-that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has levied a duty on butter coming from New Zealand. I hope that the farmers will benefit by it and that the consumer will not complain too much. Butter is, at present, too cheap; we have proof that for about one month past it has been selling below the cost price. The abrogation of the old treaty and the making of new trade arrangements with New Zealand will be highly appreciated by the citizens of this country. I congratulate the government on its attitude regarding this matter. This increase of duty on butter was based on the report submitted by the dairy industry of this country to the tariff commission, in January last. And if the present tariff is not high enough, my opinion is that it should be made higher. Butter is not a greater commodity to the consumer than other products and I know that the consumer will understand the requirements of the producer which are but just and well founded. I congratulate this government for its solicitude towards the farming class. The Liberal party has always been the champion of the farmer and workman; it has always made war on trusts which are a plague on the economic life of this, country.
The Conservative policy has always been fatal to the small capitalists; it only endorses the farmers cause during election time, and if we examine the past, we will see that the Conservatives have never done anything to protect those for whom they are claiming so much to-day. Their new attitude is but an election manoeuvre; and I hope the people of this country will understand it and that the Liberal party will be returned to power in the next parliament, with a greater majority than the one we have to-day.
