Mr. Speaker, I should be remiss in my duty to the constituency I have the honour to represent did I not commend the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. ^Dunning) upon the splendid budget that he has presented to this house and I Mr. Dumaine.]
to the country. I do not recall a time when a budget has met with such widespread expressions of approval. It would be strange indeed were it otherwise; for in summing up its salient features one cannot but conclude that the many changes effected in the tariff schedules will be beneficial to all classes and sections of our country and tend to remove the many discrepancies in our tariff rates against the countries with which we deal.
From the viewpoint of the Canadian home, it must also be conceded by every unbiased citizen that in truth this is a real householder's budget. The budget is replete with happy surprises and anticipations. In view of the abolition last year of many of the so-called nuisance taxes, the reduction of the sales tax, the decrease in revenue from import customs duties, the sum total of which is in the vicinity of 828,435,000, the large increase of expenditures necessitated by the ever-increasing demands made upon the government year by year by the people of Canada through their representatives, the payment out of current revenue of maturing bonds to the extent of 880,000,000, one would not have expected that the Minister of Finance, notwithstanding those circumstances, -would be able to submit to parliament the large surplus of $44,500,000, which, coupled with the consecutive surpluses during the last five years, has brought about a total reduction in the national debt of S257.SOO.OOO.
This, Mr. Speaker, is very heartening to the people of Canada. It makes it abundantly clear and if the present government is retained in office for a reasonable period of years-and in view of the circumstances we have no reason to doubt that such will be the case-the national debt will in the natural course of events be to the people of Canada a matter of small concern. In view of these indisputable facts, it must be admitted that the results achieved coidd have been brought about only by a wise, economic and businesslike administration of the affairs of Canada such as has been accomplished by this government.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that conditions during the last three months of the fiscal year have not been, particularly throughout western Canada, as satisfactory as could have been desired, but that was not due to any fault of the government, as some of our hon. friends opposite would have the people believe. It was due, as has already been stated in this house, to a combination of circumstances, the principal of which was the withholding of the export of wheat by that formidable western

The Budget-Mr. Bourgeois
organization known as the wheat pool. The pool was perfectly within its rights in acting as it did in an endeavour to realize a higher price for the farmers. Nevertheless this one factor alone undoubtedly reflected in large measure the depression that prevailed throughout the western provinces. It also very materially lessened the earnings of our two great railway systems. I am not condemning or condoning the wheat pool in this regard, but I must say that a corporation is indeed a formidable one that by its manipulations can affect to some extent at least, if not disorganize, the whole commercial fabric of a nation of ten million people.

My hon. friend is in a better position to speak as to that than I am.
With respect to the tariff changes made in this budget so far as the province of New Brunswick is concerned, I have no doubt that far-reaching beneficial results will follow. Living as we do beside a country of one hundred and twenty million people, with whom we have a large export trade in potatoes, lumber, pulpwood and fish, we desire the mutual good business relations between the two countries to continue. There is no sentiment throughout the maritime provinces, I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, in favour of a brick for brick tariff warfare. On the contrary, there is a sane common sense assumption that if the United States government has seen fit to adjust its tariff and make increases in its duties, it has been done in the spirit of serving the best interests of the people of that country, and therefore no one can find fault if we, actuated by the same motive of serving the best interests of our people, adopt a policy of countervailing duties, which means that countries that both buy from and sell to us have it in their power by reciprocal action on their part to enable us to reduce our duties.
The pulpwood industry in the province of New Brunswick has within recent years developed into one of great importance. We have at the present time two large pulp and paper mills, one situated at Bathurst, and another newsprint mill recently constructed in the town of Dalhousie, which is the largest of its kind in the maritime provinces, giving employment to a large number of men and affording a very substantial home market for
pulpwood. It would appear, however, and 1 am credibly informed, that there are a few large corporations throughout Canada that are desirous of having an embargo or export duty placed on pulpwood going to the United States. I want to say here and now, Mr, Speaker, that I am unalterably opposed to any movement in that direction. It would be most injurious to the farmers of New Brunswick and to others who have reserves of pulpwood. In other words, it would be placing a monopoly of purchase in the hands of a few large corporations to whom they would be obliged to sell. We desire that the farmers as well as all other exporters or dealers in pulpwood be given the opportunity of disposing of this forest product to whomsoever they desire and in the market where they can obtain the highest price.

speechtext:
That means free trade. Representing a constituency in which the basic industry is agriculture, I may say that the New Zealand trade agreement, up until the present time, has not been of much concern to the farmers and dairymen of New Brunswick, because of the fact that they have not as yet been able to meet home market requirements, but they will, I hope, in the course of a short time. However, there has recently arisen a growing sentiment in opposition to the New Zealand trade agreement in regard to butter. This opposition was expressed by resolutions passed at the annual meeting of the New Brunswick Farmers' and Dairymen's Association which met at Moncton in January last, requesting an increase of duty on butter coming from New Zealand. Nevertheless it is a fact that the New Zealand trade agreement has been of great benefit to the agricultural implement manufacturers and to the manufacturers of automobiles and other Canadian products, and also to our exporters of pulpwood. However, I am pleased that the government, in order to safeguard the best interests of the farmers, has advised the New Zealand government of its desire to terminate the agreement on the 12th of October, and that thereafter the duty on New Zealand butter entering Canada will be four cents a pound.
With respect to the increase in the British preference, no more opportune time could have been chosen in an endeavour to stimulate trade with the United Kingdom, which during the year has materially declined. Again, Mr. Speaker, has the Liberal party by action

The Budget-Mr. Bourgeois
given proof of its desire to encourage interempire trade. Not only is this desirable from the viewpoint of profit, but also as a matter of sentiment.
No better proof of the wisdom of the government in pursuance of a strong preferential trade policy could be given than is exemplified in the preferential trade agreement with the West Indies. In substantiation of this fact we have the statement of Dr. J. A. Ruddick, Dominion Dairy Commissioner, who, having returned a few days ago after a six months' visit to the West Indies, is reported in the Montreal Gazette as saying that Canadian trade is increasing tremendously, that we are now getting 90 per cent of the business in flour and more than 90 per cent of the business in dairy products, particularly cheese, butter and powdered milk, the latter trade having risen from 30 to 90 per cent within the last three years, due largely to the new preferential trade agreement between the two countries. We may now anticipate a still greater increase, particularly in fruit and vegetables, due to free entry under the preferential tariff as announced by the finance minister in his presentation of the budget. Therefore as a result the Canadian people may now exipect cheaper fruit and vegetables, particularly the people of the maritime provinces who are so geographically situated that they will benefit to a larger degree.
Coming now, Mr. Speaker, to the trend of events in the maritimes, I may say that optimism has been the keynote of expression during the last three years. It is not long since that our commercial prosperity was impeded by exorbitant freight rates and other economic burdens which confederation had imposed; but since the advent of the present government greater confidence in the future has been strikingly manifest. The claims of the maritime provinces were favourably considered by the government in the implementing of every recommendation contained in the Duncan report. The findings of the Duncan commission dealt effectively with the situation by placing the maritimes in their proper position of equality among the other provinces of the Dominion.
I desire to congratulate the government on the creation of a separate Department of Fisheries, the sole function of which will !be the advancement of the fishing industry in all its various branches. In view of this fact, I would suggest that the new Minister of Fisheries instruct his department to investigate conditions in the St. Louis river in Kent county, New Brunswick, with a view of bringing back to its former productivity its once famous oyster beds.

We are grateful for what the government has done for Kent county, particularly in the matter of public works. But there are still some much needed improvements, particularly the construction at as early a date as possible of breakwaters at Dixon's point and Moillet's gully, which are the two missing links necessary to the protection of the lives and property of our fishermen along the Northumberland strait coast of Kent county. There is also urgent need of dredging in the Buctouche and the Richibucto harbours in order to facilitate shipping. This work, I hope, will very soon 'be given favourable consideration by the present government, which we may expect will again be returned to office; for during the last nine years by its honest endeavours, it has succeeded in welding Canada into one happy, united and harmonious whole.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Canada received with great satisfaction, the budget so ably prepared by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). It answers to the needs of our country and includes all the fields of human activity. Not only does it proclaim that the financial situation of our country is in excellent shape, but its balance sheet shows a surplus of $44,507,000. The obligations contracted by the past administration, previous to December 6, 1921, have been met when they matured, without further borrowing by the King government and that, since it directs the affairs of this country, viz., close on ten years.
To fully appreciate the budget, we must consider the situation as it exists after the war, when all nations have, from the material standpoint, and more particularly from the economic standpoint, been reduced to a state of disorganization.
If we look and examine closely the present map of Europe, we note that it has almost been transformed. The various treaties while establishing peace have nevertheless created a diversity of trade interests, not only in Europe, but on the American continent. The European countries, enclosed in their new frontiers, endeavour to reestablish themselves on new trade bases. Each nation fights for its own interests, to sell its own products abroad, at the highest price obtainable, yet trying on the other hand to exclude other nations from exporting in its territory the products which might compete with its own.
Our neighbours, the United States, have sought for the last few years, to monopolize the world market and in return make the smallest trade concessions, not only to European

The Budget-Mr. Mercier (St. Henri)
countries, but to Canada, especially as regards farm products.
If in the budget, the government of this country has found it necessary to answer by countervailing rates the duties the United States put on our products, the people of the neighbouring republic cannot complain of our new tariff, because they drew it upon themselves by too much selfishness and trade exigencies on their part.
In support of this contention, not only as regards Canada but also France and certain other countries of Europe, it is only necessary to read this passage from a study on the subject, entitled: "The Tariff controversy with France" written by a distinguished economist, Mr. F. W. Taussig, in the Review of Foreign Affairs, edition of January 1928, from which I shall read the following extract:
What, then, will the United States finally do? The people of this country are recurrently called on to consider just how far they propose to carry their protectionist policy, and just how intolerant they propose to be in the way of keeping out every scrap of imported goods that might interfere with any clamorous domestic producer. Should we not consider these larger aspects of the tariff question in connection with the pending negotiations? We have proclaimed singlemindedness in tariff policy; and therein, as I have said, we are proceeding not unwisely. But does this necessarily mean complete disregard of other people? Even those who say most about holding aloof from European complications, say much also about the maintenance of friendly relations with all and the promotion of mutual good feeling. Now that we turn to a systematic policy of most-favoured-nation treatment, why not put into it some element of real favour and of genuine friendliness? It needs no acumen to discern that France does not stand alone in her feelings about our tariff rates. Other countries may make no moves such as she has made, but none the less they shrug their shoulders at the contrast between our courteous gestures and our stern realties. We are eager to export, and above all to export manufactured goods. Our Department of Commerce bends its energy to the utmost toward promoting their sales. But when others wish to send goods to us, we bend our energies to erecting barriers as high as we can devise. It *would be no bad outcome of the pending negotiations and debates if we were led to do something toward promoting beneficial trade and good relations not with France only, but with all the world?
We find in the concluding part of the speech of the Minister of Finance a true ideal of a tariff policy and trade relations of Canada with the countries of the world. From the budget there emanates a spirit of justice towards all classes of our country; it displays a spirit of fairness towards those who have invested with us considerable capital, from which the working classes may derive more benefit and better wages.
The farming classes must feel happy over the provisions of the budget, for they certainly
were taken care of; the Liberal party has always recognized that they should be protected, and at all times our policy has been: "for new and better markets."
Within the last few months, Conservative speakers have travelled across our province without success, criticizing our trade conventions with Australia and New Zealand. To please the farming class of this country, these conventions will end on October 12, 1930, when in due course, another convention will be negotiated between Canada and New Zealand. I trust that in this new treaty, provisions as advantageous as those of to-day will be included in so far as the automobiles, paper and puLpwood, are concerned.
We felt greatly satisfied, when, in the course of the present session, the various bills transferring to the Western provinces their natural resources, were adopted by the House. British Columbia also had its share in the transfer of lands, and the latter must now have more faith in the present administration of Canada which has been so generous towards it.
It was under the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then Prime Minister of Canada, that were created the western provinces, in 1905. This political Act, essentially liberal, gave them their autonomy, with the exception, however, of their lands and the administration of their natural resources.
In the year 1930, during the present session, the last of this 16th Parliament, we have witnessed with pleasure the transferring of these natural resources to the three western provinces with, besides, a readjustment of their indemnities. This generous act is to the credit of the present Prime Minister of Canada, the right hon. Mackenzie King, who has completed the work begun by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Laurier created those provinces, King liberated them completely. Their status is, to-day, that of the Eastern provinces, and it seems to me that Confederation has grown and enjoys more glory since the enactment of the various measures returning to the Western provinces their natural resources.
To foresee, sir, the end of all the economic conflicts which may at certain moments cast shadows over our destinies, is an impossibility. Surely, in the course of one's life, we must shun pessimism as much as optimism; and it is thus that necessity always succeds in equalizing things. The world is revolving and will unceasingly revolve. The world carries on without troubling about, not even listening to our speeches and, little by little, we adapt ourselves to the whims and variations of our social and political surroundings. The difficulty, however, is to reach that stage without too many clashes, and especially, without giving way to the notions and visionary

Canada is not given to new ideas and we are pleased to acknowledge that the Liberal party walks, to-day, in the footsteps of the sound traditions which it has always endorsed and which are a legacy of the political will of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It is not always wise for a member to go back to the deluge when he rises in the house to deliver a speech, but it is sometimes necessary to examine the political past of a party as that of the Liberal party to inspire oneself by the deeds of that period which brought abundance to the country, and to note with pleasure that they are always the source of prosperity and a guide for the present time, even in 1930, by applying the same principles.
If we glance over the political history of our country, we find that at the general election of 1878, the Liberal government under Mackenzie was defeated, and, during eighteen years, the Liberal party, always courageous and chivalrous, followed the barren path of the loyal opposition of Her Majesty; but at sunrise one bright morning of June, 1896, Canada again welcomed the advent to power of the Liberal party, having as its leader Sir Wilfrid Laurier. On July 13, 1896, he was sworn in as Prime Minister and took charge, with his ministers, of the destinies of Canada.
The old members of this house no doubt recall the crisis Canada experienced in 1896. Unrest was general, industries were threatened, smoke-stacks appeared like giants but lifeless, agriculture without markets, prices varied like passing clouds, the financial situation uncertain, bankruptcies, sales by sheriff numerous; all citizens faced a gloomy future. It was urgent for the Laurier government to get down immediately to work so as to stimulate business, inspire confidence in all hearts and bring back a new era of prosperity. All had to be done over again, exactly as when the King government assumed power on December 6, 1921. Laurier realized then that the situation was a difficult one, but as he had secured the people's confidence through the program he had submitted to them, he endeavoured to carry it out, notably in the west, of which he knew the needs. The western provinces, known as the Prairies, have

become since a few years, a centre of attraction; a subject of talk both in the private and political life of this country.
The birth of the Progressive politcal party, in 1921, was a matter of discussion in Canada as well as abroad. This Progressive party, which time, that great reformer, has remodelled and drawn nearer to the Liberal party in most of its ideals, always remains opposed to the Conservative party's policy.
That part of Canada, therefore, interests at present all the citizens of the Dominion. In a word, to speak of the western provinces and their numerous problems, is, as we see it, to live in the present.
The vast territory that we generally designate as the Canadian west, extends from the province of Ontario to the Pacific ocean. Its total area covers 1,114,672 square miles. Its vastness is such that, even on the geographical map of the Dominion, one cannot truly realize its size and the numerous resources it contains.
We note with pleasure that the western provinces contribute as much as Quebec, Ontario and the Maritime provinces, to make of our Canada, a great and prosperous country, enjoying the most complete social harmony, drawing the admiration of the whole of Europe and being the pride of the British Empire. But, sir, you may say, the Canadian west had a beginning, it was not always what it is to-day: prosperous and forecasting a greater future. It must have grown through the impulse of a wise administration, that government no doubt gave it its start, favoured it by its measures and legislation, finally, became aware that the west would, one day, be the granary of the empire.
You are quite right, sir, the west was opened up to colonization, farming and industry, like all other regions. The great benefactor of the west, was Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the late leader, the soul still living of the Liberal party, whose legislative acts, prudence and sincerity are still the best guide of his worthy successor, the present Prime Minister, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, our leader.
The political administration of that great statesman, was the foundation stone of the development of the west. The first factor which brought progress to the west was the adoption of the preferential tariff between England and Canada, and the trip overseas of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The latter spoke so admirably and with such frankness of his country, with such eloquence of all the advantages that it offered to the immigrants, the capitalist and manufacturer, that Canada

appeared more beautiful to the eyes of nations and especially to the English people. A brilliant future awaited those who would come to settle on the western plains. Then followed a sound immigration policy.
During the fifteen years which followed 1896, nearly 10,000 miles of railway were constructed, that is an average of two miles per day. Two transcontinentals were built, numerous branch lines were added, terminal stations were built and other branch lines in connection with shipping. Following this expansion, our country grew, and took an important place in the world. That was the doings of the Liberal party and its policy and history now repeats itself, in 1930, after more than 8 years of wise administration by the King government.
We judge of the administrative success of a country by the same standard as that of a business firm, its balance-sheet and its surplus. After two years of sound administration our government entered into a new period of surpluses. Let us quote a few figures.
For the fiscal year 1924-25, a surplus of $300,000.
For the fiscal year 1925-26, a surplus of
28,000,000.
For the fiscal year 1926-27, a surplus of $42,000,000.
For the fiscal year 1927-28, a surplus of $54,000,000.
But from this total $16,000,000 must be deducted for soldiers' lands and seeds, leaving a surplus of $38,000,000.
For the fiscal year 1928-29, a surplus of $69,782,000.
For the present fiscal year of 1929-30, a surplus of $44,507,000.
We have also reduced taxes. First, in connection with the Income tax, an innovation of the Borden government.
In 1922.-Exemption for each child, from S200 to $300.
In 1924.-Additional exemption for each child, from $300 to $500;
In 1926.-Exemption limit of the Income tax, from $2,000 to $3,000 in the case of married persons or with dependents and from $1,000 to $1,500 in other cases; moreover the tax payers whose income is $5,000 or less have but 2 per cent instead of 4 per cent to pay on taxable incomes. The income tax of large companies is reduced from 10 per cent to 9 per cent;
In 1927.-The rates of the income tax of 1926 are reduced by 10 per cent;
In 1928.-Another reduction of 10 per cent;
In 1929.-A new reduction on income tax in favour of certain companies and exemption
to the amount of $500 for those who have families to support.
The customs tariff has been changed as follows, and allow me, Sir, to quote but the most important changes:
In 1922.-Decrease of duties on sugar, farming implements, cloth, boots and shoes and certain other articles;
In 1923.-The duties on imported goods under the British preferential tariff schedule are reduced by 10 per cent each time that the regular rates of duty exceed 15 per cent and that the goods are imported directly to a Canadian port.
Decrease of duties on sugar;
In 1924.-Decrease of duties on instruments of production utilized in farming, mining, forest and fish industries;
In 1925.-Decrease of duties on well boring machinery and on motors for fishing vessels;
In 1926.-Decrease of duties on sugar, automobiles, tin, etc.
In 1928.-Numerous tariff changes inscribed at ch. 17 of the 1928 statutes;
In 1929.-Abrogation of the regulation which taxed cablegrams and other telegraph messages.
Abrogations also of the regulation which taxed railway tickets and other tickets of the same nature.
As to postage rates, the Liberals reestablished the postal rate of 2 cents, from July 1, 1926; in 1929, the same rate was established for all parts of the British Empire.
Stamp tax on cheques.
In 1922.-Tax of 2 cents levied on all cheques to the amount of $50 and a maximum tax of $2 on cheques of $5000 or over.
In 1923.-Reduction of this tax to $1.
In 1925.-Suppression of the tax on cheques to an amount not exceeding $5.
In 1927.-Decrease of the tax to a uniform rate of 2 cents on cheques over $10.
Tax on receipts.
In 1926.-Established in 1922, abolished in 1926.
It is therefore well proven that the King government never ceased from year to year to decrease the taxes. This did not hinder it from lowering considerably the national debt, as shown in the budget of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning).
Canada has made great strides, under the administration as regards to diplomatic relations with Europe and our neighbour the U. S. The High Commissioner at London and our legations at Paris, Washington and in Japan are the watchful sentries of Canadian interests and a formal act of good will towards the European countries and the neighbouring republic.
